And the second case (accusative): he went to the village by foot; he went to the city by foot; few go to heaven; or by going to heaven; the Saṅgha should be drawn back to the root, and so on.

Āsīsatthe-āyasmato dīghāyuko hotu, bhaddaṃ bhavato hotu, kusalaṃ bhavato hotu, anāmayaṃ [M 0.0148] bhavato hotu, sukhaṃ bhavato hotu, svāgataṃ bhavato hotu, attho bhavato hotu, hitaṃ bhavato hotu iccevamādi.

In the sense of wishing: May the Venerable One be long-lived; may good fortune be yours; may it be wholesome for you; may you be free from illness; may you be happy; welcome to you; may you achieve your purpose; may it be for your benefit—and so on.

Sammutippayoge– aññatra saṅghasammutiyā bhikkhussa vippavatthuṃ na vaṭṭati, sādhu sammuti me tassa bhagavato dassanāya iccevamādi.

In the usage of 'sammuti': Except by the permission of the Saṅgha, it is not proper for a bhikkhu to live apart. "Good is the permission for me to see that Blessed One"—and so on.

Bhiyyappayoge – bhiyyoso mattāyaṃ iccevamādi.

In the usage of 'bhiyya': "to a still greater extent"—and so on.

Sattamyatthe – tuyhañcassa āvi karomi, tassa me sakko pāturahosi iccevamādi.

In the sense of the locative: "I declare this to you," "Sakka appeared to me"—and so on.

Atthaggahaṇena bahūsu akkharappayogesu dissati.

By grasping the meaning, it is seen in many usages of words.

Taṃ yathā? Upamaṃ mata karissāmi, dhammaṃ vo desessāmi.

How so? I will make a comparison for you; I will teach you the Dhamma.

Sāratthe ca – desetu bhante bhagavā dhammaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ. Tassa phāsu vihārāya hoti, etassa pahiṇeyya, yathā no bhagavā byākareyya, tathāpi tesaṃ byākarissāma[M 0.0149], kappati samaṇānaṃ āyogo, amhākaṃ maṇinā attho, kimattho me buddhena, seyyo me attho, bahūpakārā bhante mahāpajā patigotamī bhagavato, bahūpakārā bhikkhave mātāpitaro puttānaṃ iccevamādi.

And in the sense of purpose: "May the Blessed One, venerable sir, teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus. It is for his comfortable dwelling. One should send for him. As the Blessed One would explain to us, so we shall explain to them. Striving is fitting for ascetics. We have need of a jewel. What need have I of the Buddha? My purpose is better. Greatly helpful, venerable sir, is Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī to the Blessed One. Greatly helpful, bhikkhus, are parents to their children"—and so on.

Sesesu akkharappayogesupi aññepi payogā payogavicakkhaṇehi yojetabbā.

And in other usages of words, further applications should be supplied by those skilled in usage.

Caggahaṇaṃ vikappanatthavāggahaṇānukaḍḍhanatthaṃ. Ye keci saddā sampadānappayogikā mayā nopadiṭṭhā, tesaṃ gahaṇatthaṃ idha vikappīyati vāsaddo.

The inclusion of 'ca' is for the purpose of drawing in the particle 'vā', which signifies an alternative. For the inclusion of whatever words applicable to the dative case that have not been taught by me, the word 'vā' is used here to provide an alternative.

Taṃ yathā? Bhikkhusaṅghassa pabhū ayaṃ bhagavā, desassa pabhū ayaṃ rājā. Khettassa pabhū ayaṃ gahapati, araññassa pabhū ayaṃ luddako iccevamādi. Kvaci dutiyā tatiyā pañcamī chaṭṭhī sattamyatthesu ca.

How so? This Blessed One is the lord of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha; this king is the lord of the country; this householder is the lord of the field; this hunter is the lord of the forest—and so on. And sometimes it is used in the sense of the second, third, fifth, sixth, or seventh case.

178, 320. Yodhāro tamokāsaṃ.

178, 320. Whatever is the support, that is the location.

Yo ādhāro, taṃ okāsasaññaṃ hoti. Svādhāro catubbidho byāpiko, opasilesiko, vesayiko sāmīpiko cāti.

Whatever is the support, that is designated as location. That support is fourfold: pervasive, contiguous, domain-based, and proximate.

Tattha [M 0.0150] byāpiko tāva–jalesu khīraṃ tiṭṭhati, tilesu telaṃ, ucchūsu raso.

Therein, the pervasive is as follows: milk exists in water, oil in sesame seeds, juice in sugarcane.

Opasilesiko–pariyaṅke rājā seti, āsane upaviṭṭho saṅgho.

The contiguous: The king lies on the couch; the Saṅgha is seated on a seat.

Vesayiko–bhūmīsu manussā caranti, antalikkhe vāyū vāyanti. Ākāse sakuṇā pakkhandanti.

The domain-based: Humans walk on the ground, winds blow in the atmosphere, birds fly in the sky.

Sāmīpiko–vane hatthino caranti, gaṅgāyaṃ ghoso tiṭṭhati, vaje gāvo duhanti, sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane.

The proximate: Elephants roam in the forest, a herdsmen's settlement is on the Ganges, cows are milked in the cow-pen, he dwells in Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove.

Okāsamiccanena kvattho? Okāse sattamī.

What is the purpose of 'okāsa'? The seventh case is used in the sense of location.

279, 292. Yena vā kayirate taṃ karaṇaṃ.

279, 292. Or, that by which something is done is the instrument.

Yena vā kayirate, yena vā passati, yena vā suṇāti, taṃ kārakaṃ karaṇasaññaṃ hoti.

Or by which something is done, or by which one sees, or by which one hears—that factor of action is designated as the instrument.

Dattena vihiṃ lunāti, vāsiyā kaṭṭhaṃ tacchati, pharasunā rukkhaṃ chindati, kudālena pathaviṃ khaṇati, satthena kammaṃ karoti. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati.

With a sickle, one reaps rice; with an adze, one carves wood; with an axe, one fells a tree; with a hoe, one digs the earth; with a knife, one performs work. With the eye, one sees forms.

Karaṇamiccanena kvattho? Karaṇe tatiyā.

What is the purpose of 'karaṇa'? The third case is used in the sense of the instrument.

280, 285. Yaṃ [M 0.0151] karoti taṃ kammaṃ.

280, 285. What one does, that is the object.

Yaṃ vā karoti, yaṃ vā passati, yaṃ vā suṇāti, taṃ kārakaṃ kammasaññaṃ hoti.

Or what one does, or what one sees, or what one hears—that factor of action is designated as the object.

Chattaṃ karoti, rathaṃ karoti, rūpaṃ passati, saddaṃ suṇāti, kaṇṭakaṃ maddati, visaṃ gilati.

One makes an umbrella, makes a chariot, sees a form, hears a sound, treads on a thorn, swallows poison.

Kammamiccanena kvattho? Kammatthe dutiyā.

What is the purpose of (the word) 'kamma'? The second case is used in the sense of the object.

281, 294. Yo karoti sa kattā.

281, 294. He who acts is the agent.

Yo karoti, so kattusañño hoti.

He who acts is designated as the agent.

Ahinā daṭṭho naro, garuḷena hato nāgo. Buddhena jito māro, upaguttena māro bandho.

A man is bitten by a snake; a nāga is slain by a garuḷa; Māra is conquered by the Buddha; Māra is bound by Upagutta.

Kattuiccanena kvattho? Kattari ca.

What is the purpose of (the word) 'kattu'? And in the sense of the agent.

282, 295. Yo kāreti sa hetu.

282, 295. He who causes another to do is the instigator.

Yo kattāraṃ kāreti, so hetusañño hoti, kattā ca.

He who causes an agent to act is designated as the instigator, and also as the agent.

So puriso taṃ purisaṃ kammaṃ kāreti so puriso tena purisena kammaṃ kāreti, so puriso tassa purisassa kammaṃ kāreti. Evaṃ hāreti pāṭheti pāceti, dhāreti.

That man causes that man to do the work; that man causes the work to be done by that man; that man causes the work for that man. Thus, one causes to carry, causes to recite, causes to cook, and causes to hold.

Hetuiccanena kvattho? Dhātūhi ṇe ṇaya ṇāpe ṇāpayā kāritāni hetvatthe.

What is the purpose of (the word) 'hetu'? From verbal roots, the causative suffixes `ṇe`, `ṇaya`, `ṇāpe`, and `ṇāpayā` are in the sense of the instigator.

283, 316. Yassa [M 0.0152] vā pariggaho taṃ sāmī.

283, 316. He whose possession it is, he is the owner.

Yassa vā pariggaho, taṃ sāmīsaññaṃ hoti.

He whose possession it is, he is designated as the owner.

Tassa bhikkhuno paṭivīso, tassa bhikkhuno patto, tassa bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ, attano mukhaṃ.

That bhikkhu's share, that bhikkhu's bowl, that bhikkhu's robe, one's own face.

Sāmīiccanena kvattho? Sāmismiṃ chaṭṭhī.

What is the purpose of (the word) 'sāmī'? The sixth case is used in the sense of the owner.

284, 283. Liṅgatthe paṭhamā.

284, 283. The first case is used in the sense of the bare stem meaning.

Liṅgatthābhidhānamatte paṭhamāvibhatti hoti.

The first case-ending occurs in the mere expression of the stem-meaning.

Puriso, purisā, eko, dve, ca, vā, he, ahe, re, are.

A man, men, one, two, and, or, ho, O, hey, alas.

285, 70. Ālapane ca.

285, 70. And in the vocative.

Ālapanatthā dhike liṅgatthābhidhānamatte ca paṭhamāvibhatti hoti.

The first case-ending occurs in the sense of addressing, which is an additional meaning to the mere expression of the stem.

Bho purisa, bhavanto purisā, bho rāja, bhavanto rājāno, he sakhe, he sakhino.

O man, O sirs, O king, O kings, O friend, O friends.

286, 291. Karaṇe tatiyā.

286, 291. The third case is used in the sense of the instrument.

Karaṇakārake tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

The third case-ending occurs in the instrumental case-relation.

Agginā kuṭiṃ jhāpeti, manasā ce paduṭṭhena, manasā ce pasannena, kāyena kammaṃ karoti.

One causes a hut to burn with fire; if with a corrupted mind, if with a serene mind; one performs action with the body.

287, 299. Sahādiyoge [M 0.0153] ca.

287, 299. And in conjunction with 'saha' and similar words.

Sahādiyogatthe ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of conjunction with 'saha' and similar words, the third case-ending occurs.

Sahāpi gaggena saṅgho uposathaṃ kareyya, vināpi gaggena, mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ, sahassena samaṃ mitā.

Even with Gagga, the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha; even without Gagga; together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus; measured as equal to a thousand.

288, 293. Kattari ca.

288, 293. And in the sense of the agent.

Kattari ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of the agent, the third case-ending occurs.

Raññā hato poso, yakkhena dinno varo, ahinā daṭṭho naro.

A man is killed by the king; a boon is given by a yakkha; a man is bitten by a snake.

289, 297. Hetvatthe ca.

289, 297. And in the sense of cause.

Hetvatthe ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of cause, the third case-ending occurs.

Annena vasati, dhammena vasati, vijjāya vasati, sakkārena vasati.

He lives by means of food; he lives by means of the Dhamma; he lives by means of knowledge; he lives by means of honor.

290, 298. Sattamyatthe ca.

290, 298. And also in the sense of the seventh case.

Sattamyatthe ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of the seventh case, the third case-ending occurs.

Tena [M 0.0154] kālena, tena samayena. (Yena kālena, yena samayena,) tena kho pana samayena.

At that time, on that occasion. (At which time, on which occasion,) then indeed, on that occasion.

291, 299. Yenaṅgavikāro.

291, 299. By which a limb is defective.

Yena byādhimatā aṅgena aṅgino vikāro lakkhīyate. Tattha tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

By which afflicted limb the defect of the one who possesses limbs is indicated. There, the third case-ending occurs.

Akkhinā kāṇo, hatthena kuṇī, kāṇaṃ passati nettena, pādena khañjo, piṭṭhiyā khujjo.

Blind in one eye; crippled in the hand; he sees the one-eyed person with his eye; lame in the foot; hunchbacked in the back.

292, 300. Visesane ca.

292, 300. And in the sense of distinction.

Visesanatthe ca tatiyāvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of distinction, the third case-ending occurs.

Gottena gotamo nātho, suvaṇṇena abhirūpo, tapasā uttamo.

By clan, the Lord is Gotama; handsome by his golden complexion; supreme through asceticism.

293, 301. Sampadāne catutthī.

293, 301. The fourth case (is used) in the sense of the recipient.

Sampadānakārake catutthīvibhatti hoti.

The fourth case-ending occurs in the recipient case-factor.

Buddhassa vā dhammassa vā saṅghassa vā dānaṃ deti, dātā hoti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā.

He gives a gift to the Buddha, or to the Dhamma, or to the Saṅgha; he is a giver to a recluse or to a brahmin.

294, 305. Namoyogādīsvapi ca.

294, 305. And also in conjunction with 'namo' and similar words.

Namoyogādīsvapi ca catutthīvibhatti hoti.

And also in conjunction with 'namo' and similar words, the fourth case-ending occurs.

Namo [M 0.0155] te buddha vīratthu, sotthi pajānaṃ, namo karohi nāgassa, svāgataṃ te mahārāja.

Homage to you, O heroic Buddha; well-being to beings; pay homage to the Nāga; welcome to you, great king.

295, 307. Apādāne pañcamī.

295, 307. The fifth case (is used) in the sense of the ablative.

Apādānakārake pañcamīvibhatti hoti.

The fifth case-ending occurs in the ablative case-factor.

Pāpā cittaṃ nivāraye, abbhā muttova candimā, bhayā muccati so naro.

One should restrain the mind from evil; like the moon freed from a cloud; that person is freed from fear.

296, 314. Kāraṇatthe ḍha.

296, 314. The fifth case (is used) in the sense of cause.

Kāraṇatthe ca pañcamīvibhatti hoti.

And in the sense of cause, the fifth case-ending occurs.

Ananubodhā appaṭivedhā catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ adassanā.

Through not awakening to, through not penetrating, through not seeing the four Noble Truths as they really are.

297, 284. Kammatthe dutiyā.

297, 284. The second case (is used) in the sense of the object.

Kammatthe dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

The second case-ending occurs in the sense of the object.

Gāvaṃ hanati, vīhayo lunāti, satthaṃ karoti, ghaṭaṃ karoti, rathaṃ karoti, dhammaṃ suṇāti, buddhaṃ pūjeti, vācaṃ bhāsatī, taṇḍulaṃ vacati, coraṃ ghāteti.

He kills a cow; he reaps rice plants; he makes a weapon; he makes a pot; he makes a chariot; he hears the Dhamma; he venerates the Buddha; he speaks a word; he cooks rice; he causes a thief to be killed.

298, 287. Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge.

298, 287. In the continuous conjunction of time and distance.

Kāladdhānaṃ accantasaṃyoge dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

In the continuous conjunction of time and distance, the second case-ending occurs.

Māsaṃ [M 0.0156] maṃsodanaṃ bhuñjati, saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī, māsaṃ sajjhāyati, yojanaṃ vanarāji, yojanaṃ dīgho pabbato, kosaṃ sajjhāyati.

He eats rice with meat for a month; the river is delightful throughout autumn; he recites for a month; a line of forest extends for a league; a mountain is a league long; he recites for a kos.

Accantasaṃyogeti kimatthaṃ? Saṃvacchare bhojanaṃ bhuñjati.

What is the purpose of 'in continuous conjunction'? He eats a meal once in a year.

299, 288. Kammappavadhanīyayutte.

299, 288. In connection with kammappavacanīyas.

Kammappavacanīyayutte dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

In connection with kammappavacanīyas, the second case-ending occurs.

Taṃ kho pana bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato, pabbajitamanupabbajiṃsu.

Indeed, concerning that Venerable Gotama, such a fair report of his fame has arisen; they went forth following him who had gone forth.

300, 286. Gati buddhi bhuja paṭha hara kara sayādīnaṃ kārite vā.

300, 286. Or in the causative of verbs of going, understanding, eating, reading, taking, making, lying down, and so on.

Gati buddhi bhuja paṭha hara kara sayādīnaṃ payoge kārite dutiyāvibhatti hoti vā.

In the causative use of verbs such as those meaning going, understanding, enjoying, reading, carrying, doing, and lying down, the second case-ending may optionally occur.

Puriso purisaṃ (gāmaṃ) gāmayati, puriso purisena vā, puriso purisassa vā. Evaṃ bodhayati, bhojayati, pāṭhayati, hārayati, kārayati, sayāpayati. Evaṃ sabbattha kārite.

A man causes a man to go (to the village); or by means of a man; or for a man. Thus: he causes to understand, causes to eat, causes to read, causes to carry, causes to do, causes to make lie down. Thus it is everywhere in the causative.

301, 215. Sāmismiṃ chaṭṭhī.

301, 215. The sixth case is used in the sense of ownership.

Sāmismiṃ chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

The sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of ownership.

Tassa [M 0.0157] bhikkhuno paṭivīso, tassa bhikkhuno patto, tassa bhikkhuno cīvaraṃ, attano mukhaṃ.

That monk's portion, that monk's bowl, that monk's robe, one's own face.

302, 319. Okāse sattamī.

302, 319. The seventh case is used in the sense of location.

Okāsakārake sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending occurs in the locative kāraka.

Gambhīre odakantike, pāpasmiṃ ramati mano, bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati kulaputto.

Near the deep water; the mind delights in evil; a clansman lives the holy life in the Blessed One.

303, 321. Sāmissarādhipati dāyāda sakkhīpatibhū pasutakusalehi ca.

303, 321. And with words meaning owner, lord, master, heir, witness, surety, devoted, and skilled.

Sāmī issara adhipati dāyāda sakkhīpatibhū pasutakusala iccetehi payoge chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.

In connection with the words sāmī (owner), issara (lord), adhipati (ruler), dāyāda (heir), sakkhī (witness), paṭibhū (surety), pasuta (devoted), and kusala (skilled), the sixth case-ending occurs, and also the seventh.

Goṇānaṃ sāmī, goṇesu sāmī, goṇānaṃ issaro, goṇesu issaro. Goṇānaṃ adhipati, goṇesu adhipati. Goṇānaṃ dāyādo, goṇesu dāyādo. Goṇānaṃ sakkhī, goṇesu sakkhī, goṇānaṃ patibhū, goṇesu patibhū. Goṇānaṃ pasuto, goṇesu pasuto. Goṇānaṃ kusalo, goṇesu kusalo.

Owner of the oxen, owner among the oxen. Lord of the oxen, lord among the oxen. Ruler of the oxen, ruler among the oxen. Heir to the oxen, heir among the oxen. Witness concerning the oxen, witness among the oxen. Guarantor for the oxen, guarantor among the oxen. Devoted to the oxen, devoted among the oxen. Skilled with oxen, skilled among oxen.

304, 322. Niddhāraṇe ca.

304, 322. And in specification.

Niddhāraṇatthe ca chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.

The sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of specification, and also the seventh.

Kaṇhā [M 0.0158] gāvīnaṃ sampannakhīratamā, kaṇhā gāvīsu sampannakhīratamā. Sāmā nārīnaṃ dassanīyatamā, sāmā nārīsu dassanīyatamā. Manussānaṃ khattiyo sūratamo, manussesu khattiyo sūratamo. Pathikānaṃ dhāvanto sīghatamo, pathikesu dhāvanto sīghatamo.

The black cow is the richest in milk of all cows; the black cow is the richest in milk among cows. The dark woman is the most beautiful of all women; the dark woman is the most beautiful among women. The warrior is the most courageous of all men; the warrior is the most courageous among men. The runner is the swiftest of all travelers; the runner is the swiftest among travelers.

305, 323. Anādare ca.

305, 323. And in disregard.

Anādare chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.

The sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of disregard, and also the seventh.

Rudato dārakassa pabbaji, rudantasmiṃ dārake pabbaji.

He went forth, disregarding the crying boy (genitive); he went forth, disregarding the crying boy (locative).

306, 289. Kvaci dutiyā chaṭṭhīnamatthe.

306, 289. Sometimes the second case is used in the sense of the sixth.

Chaṭṭhīnamatthe kvaci dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes the second case-ending occurs in the sense of the sixth.

Apissu maṃ aggivessana tisso upamā paṭibhaṃsu.

Moreover, Aggivessana, three similes occurred to me.

307, 290. Tatiyāsattamīnañca.

307, 290. And of the third and seventh.

Tatiyāsattamīnaṃ atthe ca kvaci dutiyāvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes the second case-ending occurs in the sense of the third and seventh.

Sace maṃ samaṇo gotamo ālapissati, tvañca maṃ nābhibhāsasi. Evaṃ tatiyatthe.

If the ascetic Gotama will speak with me, and you do not address me. Thus, in the sense of the third case.

Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā, ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā. Evaṃ sattamyatthe.

Having dressed in the forenoon; at one time the Blessed One... Thus, in the sense of the seventh case.

308, 317. Chaṭṭhī [M 0.0159] ca.

308, 317. And the sixth.

Tatiyāsattamīnaṃ atthe ca kvaci chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes the sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of the third and seventh cases.

Kato me kalyāṇo, kataṃ me pāpaṃ. Evaṃ tatiyatthe.

Good has been done by me; evil has been done by me. Thus, in the sense of the third case.

Kusalā naccagītassa sikkhitā cāturitthiyo, kusalo tvaṃ rathassa aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ. Evaṃ sattamyatthe.

Skilled in dance and song are the four trained women; you are skilled in the major and minor parts of the chariot. Thus, in the sense of the seventh case.

Kvacīti kimatthaṃ? Yo vo ānanda mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto, ānando atthesu vicakkhaṇo.

Why 'sometimes'? 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and the Vinaya that have been taught and laid down by me for you...' and 'Ānanda is discerning in meanings.'

309, 318. Dutiyāpañcamīnañca.

309, 318. And of the second and fifth cases.

Dutiyāpañcamīnañca atthe kvaci chaṭṭhīvibhatti hoti.

Sometimes the sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of the second and fifth cases.

Tassa bhavanti vattāro, sahasā kammassa kattāro, evaṃ dutiyatthe.

There are speakers concerning him; doers of a deed impetuously. Thus, in the sense of the second case.

Assavanatā dhammassa parihāyanti, kinnu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmi, sabbe tasanti daṇḍassa, sabbe bhāyanti maccuno, bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ, bhāyāmi ghoravisassa nāgassa. Evaṃ pañcamyatthe.

From not hearing the Dhamma, they decline. Why indeed should I fear that happiness? All tremble at the rod; all fear death. Afraid of the four terrible-poisoned snakes, I fear the terrible-poisoned nāga. Thus, in the sense of the fifth case.

310, 324. Kamma [M 0.0160] karaṇa nimittatthesu sattamī.

310, 324. The seventh case in the senses of object, instrument, and cause.

Kammakaraṇanimittatthesu sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending occurs in the senses of object, instrument, and cause.

Sundarāvuso ime ājīvakā bhikkhūsu abhivādenti. Evaṃ kammatthe.

Venerable Sundara, these Ājīvakas pay homage to the bhikkhus. Thus, in the sense of the object.

Hatthesu piṇḍāya caranti, pattesu piṇḍāya caranti, pathesu gacchanti. Evaṃ karaṇatthe.

They go for alms with their hands; they go for alms with their bowls; they go on paths. Thus, in the sense of the instrument.

Dīpi cammesu haññate, kuñjaro dantesu haññate, evaṃ nimittatthe.

The leopard is killed for its skin; the elephant is killed for its tusks. Thus, in the sense of the cause.

311, 325. Sampadāne ca.

311, 325. And in the dative.

Sampadāne ca sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending also occurs in the dative sense.

Saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphala, saṅghe gotamī dehi, saṅghe te dinne ahañceva pūjito bhavissāmi.

What is given to the Sangha is of great fruit. Gotamī, give to the Sangha. When it is given by you to the Sangha, I myself will be honored.

312, 326. Pañcamyatthe ca.

312, 326. And in the sense of the fifth case.

Pañcamyatthe ca sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending also occurs in the sense of the fifth case.

Kadalīsu gaje rakkhanti.

They protect the elephants from the banana trees.

313, 327. Kālabhāvesu ca.

313, 327. And in (expressions of) time and state.

Kālabhāvesu ca kattari payujjamāne sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending also occurs in (expressions of) time and state, when the agent is used.

Pubbaṇhasamaye [M 0.0161] gato, sāyanhasamaye āgato. Bhikkhūsu bhojīyamānesu gato, bhuttesu āgato. Gosuduyhamānesu gato, duddhāsu āgato.

He went in the forenoon; he came in the afternoon. He went while the monks were being fed; he came when they had eaten. He went while the cows were being milked; he came when they had been milked.

314, 328. Upa’jhādhikissaravacane.

314, 328. With 'upa' and 'adhi' in the sense of 'superior' and 'master'.

Upaadhiiccetesaṃ payoge adhikaissaravacane sattamīvibhatti hoti.

The seventh case-ending occurs when 'upa' and 'adhi' are used in the sense of 'superior' and 'master'.

Upa khāriyaṃ doṇo, upa nikkhe kahāpaṇaṃ. Adhi brahmadatte pañcālā, adhi naccesu gotamī, adhi devesu buddho.

A doṇa is less than a khāri; a kahāpaṇa is less than a nikkha. The Pañcālas are superior to Brahmadatta; Gotamī is superior in dances; the Buddha is superior among the gods.

315, 329. Maṇḍitu’ssukkesu tatiyā.

315, 329. The third case with 'adorned' and 'eager'.

Maṇḍitaussukkaiccetesvatthesu tatiyāvibhatti hoti, sattamī ca.

In the senses of 'adorned' and 'eager', the third case-ending occurs, and also the seventh.

Ñāṇena pasīdito, ñāṇasmiṃ vā pasīdito, ñāṇena ussukko, ñāṇasmiṃ vā ussukko tathāgato vā tathāgatagotto vā.

Pleased by knowledge, or pleased in knowledge; eager for knowledge, or eager in knowledge—whether a Tathāgata or one of the Tathāgata’s lineage.

Iti nāmakappe kārakakappo chaṭṭho kaṇḍo.

Thus ends the sixth section, the section on case relations, in the Chapter on Nouns.

Kārakakappo niṭṭhito.

The Section on Case Relations is concluded.

4. Samāsakappa

4. The Chapter on Compounds

Sattamakaṇḍa

The Seventh Section.

316, 331. Nāmānaṃ [M 0.0162] samāso yuttattho.

316, 331. A compound of nouns has a connected meaning.

Tesaṃ nāmānaṃ payujjamānapadatthānaṃ yo yuttattho, so samāsasañño hoti.

Of those nouns, the connected meaning of the words when used together is designated as a compound.

Kathinadussaṃ, āgantukabhattaṃ, jīvitindriyaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇā, sāriputtamoggallānā, brāhmaṇa gahapatikā.

Kathina cloth, food for guests, the life faculty, recluses and brahmins, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, brahmins and householders.

Nāmānamiti kimatthaṃ? Devadatto pacati, yaññadatto pacati.

Why 'of nouns'? Devadatta cooks, Yaññadatta cooks.

Yuttatthoti kimatthaṃ? Bhato rañño putto devadattassa.

Why 'connected meaning'? The king's servant is Devadatta's son.

Samāsaiccanena kvattho? Kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto.

What is the purpose of [the designation] 'compound'? Sometimes, for words that have entered into a compound, the ending is 'a'.

317, 332. Tesaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca.

317, 332. And their case endings are elided.

Tesaṃ yuttatthānaṃ samāsānaṃ vibhattiyo lopā ca honti.

Of those compounds with a connected meaning, the case endings are elided.

Kathinadussaṃ[M 0.0163], āgantukabhattaṃ.

Kathina cloth, food for guests.

Tesaṃgahaṇena samāsataddhitākhyātakitakānaṃ vibhattipaccayapadakkharāgamā ca lopā honti. Vāsiṭṭho, venateyyo.

By the inclusion of 'tesaṃ', elision of case endings, suffixes, words, letters, and augments occurs in compounds, secondary derivatives, verbs, and primary derivatives. Vāsiṭṭho, Venateyyo.

Caggahaṇa mavadhāraṇatthaṃ, pabhaṅkaro, amataddado, medhaṅkaro, dīpaṅkaro.

The inclusion of 'ca' is for emphasis: Pabhaṅkara, Amataddada, Medhaṅkara, Dīpaṅkara.

318, 333. Pakati cassa sarantassa.

318, 333. And the natural form of that which ends in a vowel [is retained].

Luttāsu vibhattīsu assa sarantassa liṅgassa pakatirūpāni honti.

When case endings are elided, the natural forms of the stem ending in a vowel remain.

Cakkhusotaṃ, mukhanāsikaṃ, rājaputto, rājapuriso.

Eye and ear, mouth and nose, a king's son, a king's man.

319, 330. Upasagganipātapubbako abyayībhāvo.

319, 330. An indeclinable compound is preceded by a prefix or particle.

Upasagganipātapubbako samāso abyayībhāvasañño hoti.

A compound preceded by a prefix or particle is designated as an indeclinable compound (avyayībhāva).

Nagarassa [M 0.0164] samīpe pavattati kathā iti upanagaraṃ, darathānaṃ abhāvo niddarathaṃ, makasānaṃ abhāvo nimmakasaṃ, vuḍḍhānaṃ paṭipāṭi yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, ye ye vuḍḍhā vā yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, jīvassa yattako paricchedo yāvajīvaṃ, cittamadhikicca pavattanti te dhammāti adhicittaṃ, pabbatassa tiro tiropabbataṃ, sotassa pati pavattati nāvā iti patisotaṃ, pāsādassa anto antopāsādaṃ.

Near the city, a story circulates—thus 'upanagaraṃ'; absence of affliction—'niddarathaṃ'; absence of mosquitoes—'nimmakasaṃ'; according to seniority—'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ'; whoever is senior—'yathāvuḍḍhaṃ'; as long as life lasts—'yāvajīvaṃ'; those qualities that arise concerning the mind—'adhicittaṃ'; beyond the mountain—'tiropabbataṃ'; a boat that goes against the stream—'patisotaṃ'; inside the palace—'antopāsādaṃ'.

Abyayībhāvamiccanena kvattho? Aṃvibhattīna makārantā abyayībhāvā.

What is the purpose of [the designation] 'avyayībhāva'? So that for avyayībhāva compounds ending in 'a', the case ending is 'aṃ'.

320, 335. So napuṃsakaliṅgo.

320, 335. It is of the neuter gender.

So abyayībhāvasamāso napuṃsakaliṅgova daṭṭhabbo.

That indeclinable compound should be regarded as being only of the neuter gender.

Kumārīsu adhikicca pavattati kathā iti adhikumāri, vadhuyā samīpe pavattati kathā iti upavadhu, gaṅgāya samīpe pavattati kathā iti upagaṅgaṃ, maṇikāya samīpe pavattati kathā iti upamaṇikaṃ.

A discussion specifically about maidens—thus 'adhikumāri'; a discussion near the bride—thus 'upavadhu'; a discussion near the Ganges—thus 'upagaṅgaṃ'; a discussion near the jewel—thus 'upamaṇikaṃ'.

321, 349. Digussekattaṃ.

321, 349. Singularity of the Dvigu compound.

Digussa samāsassa ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca.

A Dvigu compound has singularity and is of the neuter gender.

Tayo [M 0.0165] lokā tilokaṃ, tayo daṇḍā tidaṇḍaṃ, tīṇi nayanāni tinayanaṃ, tayo siṅgā tisiṅgaṃ. Catasso disā catuddisaṃ, pañca indriyāni pañcindriyaṃ.

The three worlds—'tilokaṃ'; the three staffs—'tidaṇḍaṃ'; the three eyes—'tinayanaṃ'; the three horns—'tisiṅgaṃ'. The four directions—'catuddisaṃ'; the five faculties—'pañcindriyaṃ'.

322, 359. Tathā dvande pāṇi tūriya yoggasenaṅgakhuddajantuka vividhaviruddha visabhāgatthādīnañca.

322, 359. Similarly, in a Dvanda compound, for limbs, musical instruments, implements, army divisions, small creatures, diverse and opposite things, dissimilar meanings, and so forth.

Tathā dvande samāse pāṇi tūriya yogga senaṅgakhuddajantuka vividhaviruddha visabhāgatthaiccevamādīnaṃ ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca.

Similarly, in a Dvanda compound, for limbs, musical instruments, implements, army divisions, small creatures, diverse and opposite things, dissimilar meanings, and so forth, there is singularity and the neuter gender.

Taṃ yathā? Cakkhu ca sotañca cakkhusotaṃ, mukhañca nāsikā ca mukhanāsikaṃ, chavi ca maṃsañca lohitañca chavimaṃsalohitaṃ. Evaṃ pāṇyaṅgatthe.

How is that? The eye and the ear—'cakkhusotaṃ'; the mouth and the nose—'mukhanāsikaṃ'; the skin, flesh, and blood—'chavimaṃsalohitaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of limbs.

Saṅkho ca paṇavo ca saṅkhapaṇavaṃ, gītañca vāditañca gītavāditaṃ, daddari ca ḍiṇḍimo ca daddariḍiṇḍimaṃ. Evaṃ tūriyaṅgatthe.

The conch and the drum—'saṅkhapaṇavaṃ'; singing and playing—'gītavāditaṃ'; the tambourine and the kettle-drum—'daddariḍiṇḍimaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of musical instruments.

Phālo ca pācanañca phālapācanaṃ, yugañca naṅgalañca yuganaṅgalaṃ. Evaṃ yoggaṅgatthe.

The plowshare and the goad—'phālapācanaṃ'; the yoke and the plow—'yuganaṅgalaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of implements.

Asi ca cammañca asicammaṃ, dhanu ca kalāpo ca dhanukalāpaṃ, hatthī ca asso ca hatthiassaṃ, ratho ca pattiko ca rathapattikaṃ. Evaṃ senaṅgatthe.

The sword and the shield—'asicammaṃ'; the bow and the quiver—'dhanukalāpaṃ'; the elephant and the horse—'hatthiassaṃ'; the chariot and the foot-soldier—'rathapattikaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of army divisions.

Ḍaṃsā [M 0.0166] ca makasā ca ḍaṃsamakasaṃ, kuntho ca kipilliko ca kunthakipillikaṃ, kīṭo ca sarīsapo ca kīṭasarīsapaṃ. Evaṃ khuddajantukatthe.

The gadfly and the mosquito—'ḍaṃsamakasaṃ'; the bedbug and the ant—'kunthakipillikaṃ'; the worm and the reptile—'kīṭasarīsapaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of small creatures.

Ahi ca nakulo ca ahinakulaṃ, biḷāro ca mūsiko ca biḷāramūsikaṃ, kāko ca ulūko ca kākolūkaṃ. Evaṃ vividhaviruddhatthe.

The snake and the mongoose—'ahinakulaṃ'; the cat and the mouse—'biḷāramūsikaṃ'; the crow and the owl—'kākolūkaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of various antagonists.

Sīlañca paññāṇañca sīlapaññāṇaṃ, samatho ca vipassanā ca samathavipassanaṃ, vijjā ca caraṇañca vijjācaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ visabhāgatthe.

Virtue and wisdom—'sīlapaññāṇaṃ'; serenity and insight—'samathavipassanaṃ'; knowledge and conduct—'vijjācaraṇaṃ'. Thus, in the sense of dissimilar things.

Ādiggahaṇaṃ kimatthaṃ? Dāsī ca dāso ca dāsidāsaṃ, itthī ca pumā ca itthipumaṃ, patto ca cīvarañca pattacīvaraṃ, chattañca upāhanā ca chattupāhanaṃ, tikañca catukkañca tikacatukkaṃ, veno ca rathakāro ca venarathakāraṃ, sākuṇiko ca māgaviko ca savakuṇikamāgavikaṃ, dīgho ca majjhimo ca dīghamajjhimaṃ iccevamādi.

What is the purpose of 'and so forth'? Female slave and male slave—'dāsidāsaṃ'; woman and man—'itthipumaṃ'; bowl and robe—'pattacīvaraṃ'; parasol and sandals—'chattupāhanaṃ'; three and four—'tikacatukkaṃ'; bamboo-worker and chariot-maker—'venarathakāraṃ'; fowler and deer-hunter—'sākuṇikamāgavikaṃ'; long and middle—'dīghamajjhimaṃ', and so forth.

323, 360. Vibhāsā rukkha tiṇa pasukha na dhañña janapadādīnañca.

323, 360. Optionally, for trees, grasses, livestock, wealth, grain, regions, and so forth.

Rukkhatiṇa pasu dhana dhañña janapadaiccevamādīnaṃ vibhāsā ekattaṃ hoti, napuṃsakaliṅgattañca dvande samāse. Assattho [M 0.0167] ca kapītano ca assatthakapītanaṃ, assatthakapītanā vā. Usīrañca bīraṇañca usīrabīraṇaṃ, usīrabīraṇā vā. Ajo ca eḷako ca ajeḷakaṃ, ajeḷakā vā. Hiraññañca suvaṇṇañca hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ, hiraññasuvaṇṇā vā. Sāli ca yavo ca sāliyavaṃ, sāliyavā vā. Kāsī ca kosalā ca kāsikosalaṃ, kāsikosalā vā.

For trees, grasses, livestock, wealth, grain, regions, and so forth, there is optionally singularity and the neuter gender in a Dvanda compound. The assattha and the kapītana—'assatthakapītanaṃ' or 'assatthakapītanā'. The usīra and the bīraṇa—'usīrabīraṇaṃ' or 'usīrabīraṇā'. The goat and the ram—'ajeḷakaṃ' or 'ajeḷakā'. Gold and bullion—'hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ' or 'hiraññasuvaṇṇā'. Rice and barley—'sāliyavaṃ' or 'sāliyavā'. Kāsi and Kosala—'kāsikosalaṃ' or 'kāsikosalā'.

Ādiggahaṇaṃ kimatthaṃ? Sāvajjañca anavajjañca sāvajjānavajjaṃ, sāvajjā navajjā vā. Hīnañca paṇītañca hīnapaṇītaṃ. Hīnapaṇītā vā. Kaṇho ca sukko ca kaṇhasukkaṃ, kaṇhasukkā vā.

What is the purpose of 'and so forth'? The blameworthy and the blameless—'sāvajjānavajjaṃ' or 'sāvajjānavajjā'. The inferior and the superior—'hīnapaṇītaṃ' or 'hīnapaṇītā'. The black and the white—'kaṇhasukkaṃ' or 'kaṇhasukkā'.

324, 339. Dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe kammadhārayo.

324, 339. A Karmadhāraya compound occurs when two words are in apposition.

Dve padāni tulyādhikaraṇāni yadā samasyante, tadā so samāso kammadhārayasañño hoti.

When two words in apposition are compounded, that compound is called a Karmadhāraya.

Mahanto [M 0.0168] ca so puriso cāti mahāpuriso, kaṇho ca so sappo cāti kaṇhasappo, nīlañca taṃ uppalañcāti nīluppalaṃ, lohitañca taṃ candanañcāti lohitacandanaṃ, brāhmaṇī ca sā dārikā cāti brāhmaṇadārikā, khattiyā ca sā kaññā cāti khattiyakaññā.

A great man—'mahāpuriso'; a black snake—'kaṇhasappo'; a blue lotus—'nīluppalaṃ'; red sandalwood—'lohitacandanaṃ'; a Brahmin girl—'brāhmaṇadārikā'; a Khattiya maiden—'khattiyakaññā'.

Kammadhārayaiccanena kvattho? Kammadhārayasaññe ca.

What is the purpose of 'Karmadhāraya'? For the designation 'Karmadhāraya'.

325, 348. Saṅkhyāpubbo digu.

325, 348. A Dvigu has a numeral first.

Saṅkhyāpubbo kammadhārayasamāso digusañño hoti.

A Karmadhāraya compound that has a numeral as its first member is called a Dvigu compound.

Tīṇi malāni timalaṃ, tīṇi phalāni tiphalaṃ, tayo lokā tilokaṃ, tayo daṇḍā tidaṇḍaṃ, catasso disā catuddisaṃ, pañca indriyāni pañcindriyaṃ, satta godāvariyo sattagodāvaraṃ.

Three impurities—'timalaṃ'; three fruits—'tiphalaṃ'; three worlds—'tilokaṃ'; three staffs—'tidaṇḍaṃ'; four directions—'catuddisaṃ'; five faculties—'pañcindriyaṃ'; the seven Godavaris—'sattagodāvaraṃ'.

Diguiccanena kvattho? Digusse kattaṃ.

What is the purpose of 'Dvigu'? For the singularity of the Dvigu.

326, 341. Ubhe tappurisā.

326, 341. Both are Tatpuruṣa compounds.

Ubhe digukammadhārayasamāsā tappurisasaññā honti.

Both Dvigu and Karmadhāraya compounds are called Tatpuruṣa compounds.

Na brāhmaṇo abrāhmaṇo, na vasalo avasalo, na bhikkhu abhikkhu, na pañcavassaṃ apañcavassaṃ, na [M 0.0169] pañcapūlī apañcapūlī, na sattagodāvaraṃasattagodāvaraṃ, na dasagavaṃ adasagavaṃ, na pañcagavaṃ apañcagavaṃ.

Not a Brahmin—'abrāhmaṇo'; not an outcaste—'avasalo'; not a monk—'abhikkhu'; not five years—'apañcavassaṃ'; not five bundles—'apañcapūlī'; not the seven Godavaris—'asattagodāvaraṃ'; not ten cattle—'adasagavaṃ'; not five cattle—'apañcagavaṃ'.

Tappurisaiccanena kvattho? Attaṃ nassa tappurise.

What is the purpose of 'Tatpuruṣa'? For the substitution of 'a' for 'na' in a Tatpuruṣa compound.

327, 351. Amādayo parapadebhi.

327, 351. 'Am' and so forth with subsequent words.

Tā amādayo nāmehi parapadebhi yadā samasyante, tadā so samāso tappurisasañño hoti.

When nouns with those case endings, 'am' and so forth, are compounded with subsequent words, that compound is called a Tatpuruṣa.

Bhūmiṃ gato bhūmigato, sabbarattiṃ sobhaṇo sabbarattisobhaṇo. Apāyaṃ gato apāyagato, issarena kataṃ issarakataṃ, sallena viddho sallaviddho, kathinassa dussaṃ kathinadussaṃ, āgantukassa bhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ, methunā apeto methunāpeto, corā bhayaṃ corabhayaṃ, rañño putto rājaputto, dhaññānaṃ rāsi dhaññarāsi, rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, saṃsāre dukkhaṃ saṃsāradukkhaṃ.

Gone to the earth—'bhūmigato'; beautiful all night—'sabbarattisobhaṇo'; gone to the lower realms—'apāyagato'; made by the lord—'issarakataṃ'; pierced by an arrow—'sallaviddho'; kathina cloth—'kathinadussaṃ'; food for a guest—'āgantukabhattaṃ'; abstaining from sexual intercourse—'methunāpeto'; fear of thieves—'corabhayaṃ'; son of the king—'rājaputto'; a heap of grain—'dhaññarāsi'; perception of form—'rūpasaññā'; suffering in saṃsāra—'saṃsāradukkhaṃ'.

328, 352. Aññapadatthesu bahubbīhi.

328, 352. A Bahubbīhi compound has the sense of another word.

Aññesaṃ padānaṃ atthesu dve nāmāni bahūni nāmāni yadā samasyante, tadā so samāso bahubbīhi sañño hoti.

When two or many nouns are compounded in the sense of other words, then that compound is known as a Bahubbīhi.

Āgatā [M 0.0170] samaṇā imaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ soyaṃ āgatasamaṇo, saṅghārāmo. Jitāni indriyāni anena samaṇena soyaṃ jitindriyo, samaṇo. Dinno suṅko yassa rañño soyaṃ dinnasuṅko, rājā. Niggatā janā asmā gāmā soyaṃ niggatajano, gāmo. Chinno hatto yassa purisassa soyaṃ chinnahattho, puriso. Sampannāni sassāni yasmiṃ janapade soyaṃ sampannasasso, janapado.

Ascetics have come to this monastery—this is the monastery 'to which ascetics have come' (āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo). The senses have been conquered by this ascetic—this is the ascetic 'by whom the senses have been conquered' (jitindriyo samaṇo). A tax has been given to this king—this is the king 'to whom a tax has been given' (dinnasuṅko rājā). People have departed from this village—this is the village 'from which people have departed' (niggatajano gāmo). This man's hand has been cut—this is the man 'whose hand has been cut' (chinnahattho puriso). Crops are abundant in this country—this is the country 'in which crops are abundant' (sampannasasso janapado).

Nigrodhassa parimaṇḍalo nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo, nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo iva parimaṇḍalo yo rājakumāro soyaṃ nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo. Atha vā nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo iva parimaṇḍalo yassa rājakumārassa soyaṃ nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo, rājakumāro.

The roundness of a banyan tree is `nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo`. The prince who is round like the roundness of a banyan tree is `nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo`. Or, the prince whose roundness is like the roundness of a banyan tree is `nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo`, the prince.

Cakkhuno bhūto cakkhubhūto, cakkhubhūto iva bhūto yo bhagavā soyaṃ cakkhubhūto, bhagavā.

One who has become the eye is `cakkhubhūto`. The Blessed One who has become like one who has become the eye—he is `cakkhubhūto`, the Blessed One.

Suvaṇṇassa vaṇṇo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, suvaṇṇavaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa bhagavato soyaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, bhagavā.

The color of gold is `suvaṇṇavaṇṇo`. The Blessed One whose color is like the color of gold—he is `suvaṇṇavaṇṇo`, the Blessed One.

Brahmuno saro brahmassaro, brahmassaro viya saro yassa bhagavato soyaṃ brahmassaro, bhagavā.

The voice of Brahmā is `brahmassaro`. The Blessed One whose voice is like the voice of Brahmā—he is `brahmassaro`, the Blessed One.

Sayaṃ [M 0.0171] patita paṇṇa pupphaphalavāyutoyāhārāti paṇṇañca pupphañca phalañca paṇṇapupphaphalāni, sayameva patitāni sayaṃpatitāni, sayaṃpatitāni ca tāni paṇṇapupphaphalāni ceti sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalāni vāyu ca toyañca vāyutoyāni, sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalāni ca vāyutoyāni ca sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāni. Sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāni āhārā yesaṃ te sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā, isayo. Yamettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Ayaṃ pana dvandakammadhārayagabbho tulyādhikaraṇapahubbīhi.

Sayaṃ patita paṇṇa pupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā (whose food is self-fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water). Leaves and flowers and fruits are paṇṇapupphaphalāni. Self-fallen are sayaṃpatitāni. And those self-fallen leaves-flowers-fruits are sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalāni. Wind and water are vāyutoyāni. And self-fallen leaves-flowers-fruits and wind-water are sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāni. Those whose food is sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāni—they are 'those whose food is self-fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water' (sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā), the sages. Whatever should be said here has already been said below. This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Dvandva and Kammadhāraya compounds.

Atha vā – sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyehi āhārā yesaṃ te sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or—those whose food is by means of self-fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water—they are 'those whose food is by means of self-fallen leaves, flowers, fruits, wind, and water' (sayaṃpatitapaṇṇapupphaphalavāyutoyāhārā). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a different referent.

Nānā dumapatita pupphavāsita sānūti nānāpakārā dumā nānādumā, nānādumehi patitāni nānādumapati tāni, nānādumapatitāni ca tāni pupphāni ceti nānādumapatitapupphāni, nānādumapatitapupphehi vāsitā nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā, nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā sānū yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana kammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Nānā dumapatita pupphavāsita sānū (whose slopes are fragrant with flowers fallen from various trees). Various kinds of trees are nānādumā. Fallen from various trees are nānādumapatitāni. And those flowers fallen from various trees are nānādumapatitapupphāni. Scented by flowers fallen from various trees is nānādumapatitapupphavāsitā. The mountain king whose slopes are scented by flowers fallen from various trees—he is 'one whose slopes are scented by flowers fallen from various trees' (nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu), the mountain king. This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Kammadhāraya and Tatpurisa compounds.

Atha [M 0.0172] vā – vāsitā sānū vāsitasānu, sāpekkhatte satipi gamakattā samāso. Nānādumapatitapupphehi vāsitasānū yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or—'scented slopes' (vāsitasānu): even though there is dependency, it is a compound because it conveys the meaning. The mountain king whose scented slopes are by means of flowers fallen from various trees—he is 'one whose slopes are scented by flowers fallen from various trees' (nānādumapatitapupphavāsitasānu), the mountain king. This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a different referent.

Byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭoti ambuṃ dhāretīti ambudharo, ko so? Pajjunno. Vividhā ālambo byālambo, byālambo ca so ambudharo cāti byālambambudharo, byālambambudharassa bindū byālambambudharabindū, byālambambudharabindūhi cumbito byālambambudharabinducumbito, byālambamburebinducumbito kūṭo yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo. Ayaṃ pana kammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo (whose peaks are kissed by drops from hanging clouds). He who holds water is ambudharo (water-holder)—who is that? Pajjunna (the rain-god). Various supports are byālambo (hanging/suspended). And that which is hanging and a water-holder is byālambambudharo (hanging cloud). The drops of the hanging cloud are byālambambudharabindū. Kissed by the hanging-cloud-drops is byālambambudharabinducumbito. The mountain king whose peaks are kissed by hanging-cloud-drops—he is 'one whose peaks are kissed by hanging-cloud-drops' (byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Kammadhāraya and Tatpurisa compounds.

Atha vā – cumbito kūṭo cumbitakūṭo, sāpekkhatte satipi gamakattā samāso. Byālambambudharabindūhi cumbitakūṭo yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or—'kissed peak' (cumbitakūṭo): even though there is dependency, it is a compound because it conveys the meaning. The mountain king whose peak is kissed by hanging-cloud-drops—he is 'one whose peak is kissed by hanging-cloud-drops' (byālambambudharabinducumbitakūṭo). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a different referent.

Amita bala parakkamajutīti na mitā amitā, balañca parakkamo ca juti ca balaparakkamajutiyo, amitā balaparakkamajutiyo yassa soyaṃ amitabalaparakkamajuti, ayaṃ pana kammadhārayadvandagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Amita bala parakkamajuti (whose strength, exertion, and splendor are immeasurable). Not measured are amitā (immeasurable). Strength and exertion and splendor are balaparakkamajutiyo. He whose strength-exertion-splendor are immeasurable—he is 'one whose strength, exertion, and splendor are immeasurable' (amitabalaparakkamajuti). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Kammadhāraya and Dvandva compounds.

Pīṇorakkhaṃsa [M 0.0173] bāhūti uro ca akkhañca aṃso ca bāhu ca urakkhaṃsabāhavo, pīṇā urakkhaṃsabāhavo yassa bhagavato soyaṃ pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu. Ayaṃ pana dvandavabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu (whose chest, eyes, shoulders, and arms are plump). Chest and eye and shoulder and arm are urakkhaṃsabāhavo. The Blessed One whose chest-eye-shoulder-arms are plump—he is 'one whose chest, eyes, shoulders, and arms are plump' (pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing a Dvandva compound.

Pīṇa gaṇḍa vadana thanūrujaghanāti gaṇḍo ca vadanañca thano ca ūru ca jaghanañca gaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā, pīṇā gaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā yassā sāyaṃ pīṇagaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā. Ayampi dvandagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Pīṇa gaṇḍa vadana thanūrujaghanā (whose cheeks, face, breasts, thighs, and buttocks are plump). Cheek and face and breast and thigh and buttock are gaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā. She whose cheeks-face-breasts-thighs-buttocks are plump—she is 'one whose cheeks, face, breasts, thighs, and buttocks are plump' (pīṇagaṇḍavadanathanūrujaghanā). This too is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing a Dvandva compound.

Vavara surāsura garuḍa manuja bhujaga gandhabba makuṭa kūṭa cumbita selasaṅghaṭṭita caraṇoti surā ca asurā ca garuḍā ca manujā ca bhujagā ca gandhabbā ca surāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbā, pavarā ca te surāsuragaruḍamanujabhujaga gandhabbā ceti pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbā, pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbānaṃ makuṭāni pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭāni, pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭānaṃ kūṭāni pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭāni, pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭesu cumbitā pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitā, pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitā ca te selā cāti pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselā, pavarasurāsura garuḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselehi saṅghaṭṭitā pavarasurāsura garuḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitā, pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitā caraṇā yassa tathāgatassa soyaṃ [M 0.0174] pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitacaraṇo, tathāgato, ayaṃ pana dvandakammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Pavara surāsura garuḍa manuja bhujaga gandhabba makuṭa kūṭa cumbita selasaṅghaṭṭita caraṇo (whose feet are struck by rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas). Gods and asuras and garuḍas and humans and nāgas and gandhabbas are surāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbā. And those excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbā. The crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭāni. The tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭāni. Kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitā. And those rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselā. Struck by the rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas are pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitā. The Tathāgata whose feet are struck by rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas—he is 'one whose feet are struck by rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas' (pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitacaraṇo), the Tathāgata. This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Dvandva, Kammadhāraya, and Tatpurisa compounds.

Atha vā–saṅghaṭṭitā caraṇā saṅghaṭṭitacaraṇā, sāpekkhatte satipi gamakattā samāso. Pavarasurāsura garuḍamanujabhujaga gandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselehi saṅghaṭṭitacaraṇā yassa tathāgatassa soyaṃ pavarasurāsuragaruḍa manujabhujaga gandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭita caraṇo. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or—'struck feet' (saṅghaṭṭitacaraṇā): even though there is dependency, it is a compound because it conveys the meaning. The Tathāgata whose struck feet are by means of rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods-asuras-garuḍas-humans-nāgas-gandhabbas—he is 'one whose feet are struck by rocks kissed by the tips of the crowns of the excellent gods, asuras, garuḍas, humans, nāgas, and gandhabbas' (pavarasurāsuragaruḍamanujabhujagagandhabbamakuṭakūṭacumbitaselasaṅghaṭṭitacaraṇo). This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a different referent.

Catuddisoti catasso disā yassa soyaṃ catuddiso, bhagavā.

Catuddiso (four-directional). He who has the four directions—he is 'four-directional' (catuddiso), the Blessed One.

Pañcacakkhūti pañca cakkhūni yassa tathāgatassa soyaṃ pañcacakkhu, tathāgato.

Pañcacakkhu (five-eyed). The Tathāgata who has five eyes—he is 'five-eyed' (pañcacakkhu), the Tathāgata.

Dasabaloti dasa balāni yassa soyaṃ dasabalo, bhagavā.

Dasabalo (ten-powered). He who has ten powers—he is 'ten-powered' (dasabalo), the Blessed One.

Anantañāṇoti nassa anto anantaṃ, anantaṃ ñāṇaṃ yassa tathāgatassa soyaṃ anantañāṇo, tathāgato.

Anantañāṇo (of immeasurable knowledge). That which has no end is ananta (immeasurable). The Tathāgata whose knowledge is immeasurable—he is 'one of immeasurable knowledge' (anantañāṇo), the Tathāgata.

Amita ghana sarīroti na mitaṃ amitaṃ, ghanaṃ eva sarīraṃ ghanasarīraṃ, amitaṃ ghanasarīraṃ yassa tathāgatassa soyaṃ amitaghanasarīro, tathāgato.

Amita ghana sarīro (of immeasurable and compact body). Not measured is amita (immeasurable). Indeed a compact body is ghanasarīra. The Tathāgata whose compact body is immeasurable—he is 'one of immeasurable and compact body' (amitaghanasarīro), the Tathāgata.

Amita bala parakkama pattoti na mitā amitā, balañca parakkamo ca balaparakkamā, amitā eva balaparakkamā amitabalaparakkamā[M 0.0175], amitabalaparakkamā pattā yena soyaṃ amitabalaparakkamapatto, bhagavā. Ayaṃ pana kammadhārayadvandagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Amita bala parakkama patto (who has attained immeasurable strength and exertion). Not measured are amitā (immeasurable). Strength and exertion are balaparakkamā. Indeed immeasurable strength-exertion are amitabalaparakkamā. He by whom immeasurable strength-exertion has been attained—he is 'one who has attained immeasurable strength and exertion' (amitabalaparakkamapatto), the Blessed One. This, however, is a Bahubbīhi compound with a common referent, containing Kammadhāraya and Dvandva compounds.

Matta bhamara gaṇa cumbita vikasitapupphavallināgarukkho pasobhita kandaroti mattā eva bhamarā mattabhamarā, mattabhamarānaṃ gaṇā mattabhamaragaṇā, mattabhamaragaṇehi cumbitāni mattabhamaraṇacumbitāni, vikasitāni eva pupphāni vikasitapupphāni, mattabhamaragaṇacumbitāni vikasitapupphāni yesaṃ tehi mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphā, valli ca nāgarukkho ca mallināgarukkhā, mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphā ca te vallināgarukkhā ceti mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkhā, mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkhehi upasobhitāni mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkho pasobhitāni, mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkho pasobhitāni kandarāni yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapuppha vallināgarukkho paso bhitakandaro, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana dvandakammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

The mountain caves are adorned with flowering creepers and Nāga trees, kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees. 'Intoxicated' are the bees, hence 'intoxicated bees'; the swarms of intoxicated bees are 'swarms of intoxicated bees'; kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees are 'kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees'; 'blossomed' are the flowers, hence 'blossomed flowers'; those which have blossomed flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees are 'having blossomed flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees'; creepers and Nāga trees are 'creepers-and-Nāga-trees'; those creepers and Nāga trees which have blossomed flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees are 'creepers-and-Nāga-trees with blossomed flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees'; adorned with creepers and Nāga trees whose blossomed flowers are kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees are 'adorned with creepers-and-Nāga-trees with blossomed flowers kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees'; that king of mountains whose caves are adorned with creepers and Nāga trees whose blossomed flowers are kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees is this 'king of mountains with caves so adorned'. This, however, is an appositional bahubbīhi compound containing dvanda, kammadhāraya, and tatpurisa elements.

Atha vā–upasobhitāni kandarāni upasobhitakandarāni, sāpekkhatte satipi gamakattā samāso. Mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkhehi upasobhitakandarāni yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ mattabhamaragaṇacumbitavikasitapupphavallināgarukkho pasobhitakandaro, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or alternatively—'adorned caves' are 'adorned-caves'; the compound is formed because the meaning is conveyed, even if there is a dependency. That king of mountains whose caves are adorned with flowering creepers and Nāga trees kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees is this 'king of mountains with caves adorned by flowering creepers and Nāga trees kissed by swarms of intoxicated bees'. This, however, is a bahubbīhi compound with different referents.

Nānā [M 0.0176] rukkha tiṇa patita pupphopasobhita kandaroti rukkho ca tiṇañca rukkhatiṇāni, nānā pakārāni eva rukkhatiṇāni nānārukkhatiṇāni, nānārukkhatiṇehi patitāni nānārukkhatiṇapatitāni, nānārukkhatiṇapatitāni ca tāni pupphāni ceti nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphāni, nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphehi upasobhitāni nānārukkhatiṇapatita pupphopasobhitāni, nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphopasobhitāni kandarāni yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphopasobhitakandaro, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana dvandakammadhārayatappurisagabbho tulyādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

The mountain caves are adorned with flowers fallen from various trees and grasses. 'Trees' and 'grasses' are 'trees-and-grasses'; 'of various kinds' are those trees-and-grasses, hence 'various-trees-and-grasses'; fallen from various-trees-and-grasses are 'fallen-from-various-trees-and-grasses'; those flowers fallen from various-trees-and-grasses are 'flowers-fallen-from-various-trees-and-grasses'; adorned with flowers fallen from various-trees-and-grasses are 'adorned-with-flowers-fallen-from-various-trees-and-grasses'; that king of mountains whose caves are adorned with flowers fallen from various-trees-and-grasses is this 'king of mountains with caves so adorned'. This, however, is an appositional bahubbīhi compound containing dvanda, kammadhāraya, and tatpurisa elements.

Atha vā–upasobhitāni eva kandarāni upasobhitakandarāni, (sāpekkhatte satipi gamakattā samāso.) Nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphehi upasobhitakandarāni yassa pabbatarājassa soyaṃ nānārukkhatiṇapatitapupphopasobhitakandaro, pabbatarājā. Ayaṃ pana bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Or alternatively—'adorned caves' are indeed 'adorned-caves' (the compound is formed because the meaning is conveyed, even if there is a dependency). That king of mountains whose caves are adorned with flowers fallen from various trees and grasses is this 'king of mountains with caves adorned with flowers fallen from various trees and grasses'. This, however, is a bahubbīhi compound with different referents.

Nānā musala phāla pabbata taru kaliṅgara sara dhanugadāsi tomarahatthāti musalo ca phālo ca pabbato ca taru ca kaliṅgaro ca saro ca dhanu ca gadā caasi ca tomaro, ca musalaphālapabbatatarukaliṅgarasaradhanugadāsitomarā, nānā pakārā eva musalaphālapabbatatarukaliṅgarasaradhanugadāsitomarā nānāmusalaphālapabbatatarukaliṅgarasaradhanugadāsitomarā, nānāmusalaphālapabbatatarukaliṅgarasaradhanugadāsitomarā hatthesu [M 0.0177] yesaṃ te nānāmusalaphālapabbatatarukaliṅgara saradhanugadāsitomarahatthā. Ayaṃ pana dvandakammadhārayagabbho bhinnādhikaraṇabahubbīhi.

Those with various mallets, ploughshares, mountains, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and spears in hand. This is analyzed as: 'mallet' and 'ploughshare' and 'mountain' and 'tree' and 'log' and 'arrow' and 'bow' and 'club' and 'sword' and 'spear' are 'mallet-ploughshare-mountain-tree-log-arrow-bow-club-sword-and-spear'; 'of various kinds' are those mallets, ploughshares, mountains, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and spears, hence 'various-mallets-ploughshares-mountains-trees-logs-arrows-bows-clubs-swords-and-spears'; those who have various mallets, ploughshares, mountains, trees, logs, arrows, bows, clubs, swords, and spears in their hands are 'those-with-various-mallets-ploughshares-mountains-trees-logs-arrows-bows-clubs-swords-and-spears-in-hand'. This, however, is a non-appositional bahubbīhi compound containing dvanda and kammadhāraya elements.

Bahubbīhi iccanena kvattho? Bahubbīhimhi ca.

What is the purpose of the term 'bahubbīhi'? And in the case of a 'bahubbīhi'.

329, 357. Nāmānaṃ samuccayo dvando.

329, 357. A collection of nouns is a dvanda.

Nāmānaṃ ekavibhattikānaṃ yo samuccayo, so dvandasañño hoti.

The collection of nouns having the same case ending is called a dvanda.

Candimā ca sūriyo ca candimasūriyā, samaṇo ca brāhmaṇo ca samaṇabrāhmaṇā, sāriputto ca moggallāno ca sāriputtamoggallānā, brāhmaṇo ca gahapatiko ca brāhmaṇagahapatikā, yamo ca varuṇo ca yamavaruṇā, kuvero ca vāsavo ca kuveravāsavā.

The moon and the sun are 'candimasūriyā'; the ascetic and the brahmin are 'samaṇabrāhmaṇā'; Sāriputta and Moggallāna are 'sāriputtamoggallānā'; the brahmin and the householder are 'brāhmaṇagahapatikā'; Yama and Varuṇa are 'yamavaruṇā'; Kuvera and Vāsava are 'kuveravāsavā'.

Dvandaiccanena kvattho? Dvandaṭṭhā vā.

What is the purpose of the term 'dvanda'? Or in the sense of a pair.

330, 340. Mahataṃ mahā tulyādhikaraṇe pade.

330, 340. 'mahā' for 'mahanta' before an appositional term.

Tesaṃ mahantasaddānaṃ mahāādeso hoti tulyādhikaraṇe pade.

For the word 'mahanta', the substitution 'mahā' occurs before an appositional term.

Mahanto [M 0.0178] ca so puriso cāti mahāpuriso, mahantī ca sā devī cāti mahādevī, mahantañca taṃ balañcāti mahābalaṃ, mahanto ca so nāgo cāti mahānāgo, mahanto ca so yaso cāti mahāyaso, mahantañca taṃ padumavanañcāti mahāpadumavanaṃ, mahantī ca sā nadī cāti mahānadī, mahanto ca so maṇi cāti mahāmaṇi, mahanto ca so gahapatiko cāti mahāgahapatiko, mahantañca taṃ dhanañcāti mahādhanaṃ, mahanto ca so puñño cāti mahāpuñño.

A great man is 'mahāpuriso'; a great goddess is 'mahādevī'; great power is 'mahābalaṃ'; a great elephant is 'mahānāgo'; great glory is 'mahāyaso'; a great lotus grove is 'mahāpadumavanaṃ'; a great river is 'mahānadī'; a great jewel is 'mahāmaṇi'; a great householder is 'mahāgahapatiko'; great wealth is 'mahādhanaṃ'; great merit is 'mahāpuñño'.

Bahuvacanaggahaṇena kvaci mahanta saddassa mahādeso hoti. Mahantañca taṃ phalañcāti mahapphalaṃ, mahabbalaṃ, evaṃ mahaddhanaṃ, mahabbhayaṃ.

By the taking of the plural form in the sutta, sometimes the substitution for the word 'mahanta' is 'maha'. Great fruit is 'mahapphalaṃ'; great strength is 'mahabbalaṃ'; similarly, great wealth is 'mahaddhanaṃ'; great fear is 'mahabbhayaṃ'.

331, 353. Itthiyaṃ bhāsitapumitthī pumāva ce.

331, 353. A feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form is treated as masculine if it is the first member of a compound.

Itthiyaṃ tulyādhikaraṇe pade ce bhāsitapumitthī pumāva daṭṭhabbā.

In an appositional compound, a feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form is to be regarded as masculine.

Dīghā jaṅghā yassa soyaṃ dīghajaṅgho, kalyāṇabhariyo, pahūtapañño.

He whose legs are long is 'dīghajaṅgho'; one with a good wife is 'kalyāṇabhariyo'; one of abundant wisdom is 'pahūtapañño'.

Bhāsitapupeti [M 0.0179] kimatthaṃ? Brāhmaṇabandhu ca sā bhariyā cātibrāhmaṇabandhubhariyā.

Why the specification 'that has a corresponding masculine form'? A kinswoman of a brahmin who is a wife is 'brāhmaṇabandhubhariyā'.

332, 343. Kammadhārayasaññe ca.

332, 343. And in a kammadhāraya compound.

Kammadhārayasaññe ca samāse itthiyaṃ tulyādhikaraṇe pade pubbe bhāsitapumitthī ce, pumāva daṭṭhabbā. Brāhmaṇadārikā, khattiyakaññā, khattiyakumārikā.

And in a compound termed kammadhāraya, if the first member in apposition is a feminine word that has a corresponding masculine form, it is to be regarded as masculine. For example: 'brāhmaṇadārikā', 'khattiyakaññā', 'khattiyakumārikā'.

Bhāsitapumeti kimatthaṃ? Khattiyabandhudārikā, brāhmaṇabandhudārikā.

Why the specification 'that has a corresponding masculine form'? 'khattiyabandhudārikā', 'brāhmaṇabandhudārikā'.

333, 344. Attaṃ nassa tappurise.

333, 344. 'a' for 'na' in a tatpurisa compound.

Nassa padassa tappurise uttarapade attaṃ hoti.

In a tatpurisa compound, 'a' is substituted for the word 'na' before the following term.

Nabrāhmaṇo abrāhmaṇo, avasalo, abhikkhu, apañcavassaṃ, apañcagavaṃ.

'na brāhmaṇo' becomes 'abrāhmaṇo' (a non-brahmin); 'avasalo' (not an outcaste); 'abhikkhu' (not a monk); 'apañcavassaṃ' (not five years); 'apañcagavaṃ' (not five cows).

334, 345. Sare ana.

334, 345. 'an' before a vowel.

Nassa padassa tappurise ana ādeso hoti sare pare.

In a tatpurisa compound, 'an' is substituted for the word 'na' when a vowel follows.

Na asso anasso, anissaro, anariyo.

'na asso' becomes 'anasso' (not a horse); 'anissaro' (not a lord); 'anariyo' (not noble).

335, 346. Kada [M 0.0180] kussa.

335, 346. 'kad' for 'ku'.

Kuiccetassa kada hoti sare pare.

'kad' is substituted for 'ku' when a vowel follows.

Kucchitaṃ annaṃ kadannaṃ, kucchitaṃ asanaṃ kadassanaṃ.

Bad food is 'kadannaṃ'; bad eating is 'kadassanaṃ'.

Sareti kimatthaṃ? Kucchitā dārā yesaṃ (apuññakārānaṃ) te hontīti kudārā, kujanā. Evaṃ kuputtā, kugehā, kuvatthā, kudāsā.

For what purpose is `sare` [when a vowel follows] stated? Those whose wives are contemptible (of those who perform demeritorious deeds) are `kudārā`; `kujanā` (contemptible people). Similarly, `kuputtā` (contemptible sons), `kugehā` (contemptible houses), `kuvatthā` (contemptible clothes), `kudāsā` (contemptible slaves).

336, 347. Kā’ppatthesu ca.

336, 347. And `kā` in the sense of disparagement.

Kuiccetassa kā hoti appatthesu ca.

`Kā` is substituted for `ku` also in the sense of disparagement.

Kālavaṇaṃ, kāpupphaṃ.

`Kālavaṇaṃ` (contemptible salt); `kāpupphaṃ` (contemptible flower).

Bahuvacanaggahaṇaṃ kimatthaṃ? Kuiccetassa anappatatthesupi kvaci kā hoti, kāpurisā.

For what purpose is the plural form specified? Sometimes `kā` is substituted for `ku` even in senses other than disparagement, for example, `kāpurisā` (contemptible men).

337, 350. Kvaci samāsantagatānamakāranto.

337, 350. Sometimes, the final vowel of the final member of a compound becomes `a`.

Samāsantagatānaṃ nāmānamanto saro kvaci akāro hoti.

Of nouns at the end of a compound, the final vowel sometimes becomes `a`.

Devānaṃ rājā devarājo, devarājā, devānaṃ sakhā devasakho, devasakhā, pañca ahāni pañcāhaṃ, sattāhaṃ, pañcagavaṃ, chattupāhanaṃ, upasaradaṃ, visālakkho, vimukho.

King of the gods: `devarājo`, `devarājā`; friend of the gods: `devasakho`, `devasakhā`; five days: `pañcāhaṃ`; seven days: `sattāhaṃ`; five cows: `pañcagavaṃ`; umbrella and shoes: `chattupāhanaṃ`; near autumn: `upasaradaṃ`; wide-eyed: `visālakkho`; with face averted: `vimukho`.

Kāraggahaṇaṃ [M 0.0181] kimatthaṃ? Ākāranta ikārantā ca honti, paccakkhā dhammā yassa soyanti paccakkhadhammā, surabhino gandho surabhigandhi, sundaro gandho sugandhi, pūtino gandho pūtigandhi, kucchito gandho kugandhi, duṭṭhu gandho yassa soyanti dugandhi, pūti eva gandho pūtigandhi.

For what purpose is the inclusion of `-kāra` [in `akāranto`]? Because they also end in `ā` and `i`. He for whom the teachings are manifest is `paccakkhadhammā`; fragrant scent: `surabhigandhi`; beautiful scent: `sugandhi`; foul scent: `pūtigandhi`; contemptible scent: `kugandhi`; he whose scent is bad is `dugandhi`; a scent that is simply foul: `pūtigandhi`.

Nadīantā ca kattuantā ca kapaccayo hoti samāsante.

The suffix `ka` is added at the end of a compound to stems ending in `nadī` and `kattu`.

Bahū nadiyo yasmiṃ soyaṃ bahunadiko, janapado. Bahavo kattāro yassa soyaṃ bahukattuko, puriso.

That in which there are many rivers is `bahunadiko`, a region. He who has many agents is `bahukattuko`, a man.

338, 356. Nadimhā ca.

338, 356. And from `nadī`.

Nadimhā ca kapaccayo hoti samāsante.

And from a stem of the `nadī` class, the suffix `ka` is added at the end of a compound.

Bahū nadiyo yasmiṃ soyanti bahunadiko. Bahū kantiyo yassa soyanti bahukantiko. Bahunāriko.

That in which there are many rivers is `bahunadiko`. He who has many beloved women is `bahukantiko`. Similarly, `bahunāriko`.

339, 358. Jāyāya tudaṃ jāni patimhi.

339, 358. For `jāyā`, `tudaṃ` and `jāni` when `pati` follows.

Jāyāiccetāya tudaṃ jāniiccete ādesā honti patimhi pare.

For the word `jāyā`, `tudaṃ` and `jāni` are the substitutes when `pati` follows.

Tudaṃpatī, jānipatī.

`Tudaṃpatī`, `jānipatī`.

340, 355. Dhanumhā ca.

340, 355. And from `dhanu`.

Dhanumhā ca āpaccayo hoti samāsante.

And from `dhanu`, the suffix `ā` is added at the end of a compound.

Gāṇḍīvo [M 0.0182] dhanu yassa soyaṃ gāṇḍīvadhanvā.

He whose bow is Gāṇḍīva is `gāṇḍīvadhanvā`.

341, 336. Aṃ vibhattīnamakārantā abyayībhāvā.

341, 336. From an `avyayībhāva` compound ending in `a`, `aṃ` is substituted for the case endings.

Tasmā akārantā abyayībhāvasamāsā parāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ kvaci aṃ hoti.

Therefore, after an `avyayībhāva` compound ending in `a`, the following case endings sometimes become `aṃ`.

Adhicittaṃ, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ, upakumbhaṃ, yāvajīvaṃ, tiropabbataṃ, tiropākāraṃ, tirokuṭṭaṃ, antopāsādaṃ.

`Adhicittaṃ`: concerning the mind; `yathāvuḍḍhaṃ`: according to seniority; `upakumbhaṃ`: near the pot; `yāvajīvaṃ`: for life; `tiropabbataṃ`: beyond the mountain; `tiropākāraṃ`: beyond the wall; `tirokuṭṭaṃ`: beyond the rampart; `antopāsādaṃ`: inside the palace.

Kvacīti kimatthaṃ? Adhicittassa bhikkhuno.

For what purpose is `kvaci` (sometimes) stated? As in `adhicittassa bhikkhuno` (of a monk of heightened mind).

342, 337. Saro rasso napuṃsake.

342, 337. In the neuter, the vowel is short.

Napuṃsake vattamānassa abyayībhāvasamāsassa liṅgassa saro rasso hoti.

The final vowel of the stem of an `avyayībhāva` compound, when it is in the neuter, becomes short.

Kumārīsu adhikicca pavattati kathā iti adhikumāri. Upavadhu, upagaṅgaṃ, upamaṇikaṃ.

`Adhikumāri` means a talk that proceeds concerning maidens. Similarly, `upavadhu`, `upagaṅgaṃ`, `upamaṇikaṃ`.

343, 338. Aññasmā lopo ca.

343, 338. And from others, elision.

Aññasmā abyayībhāvasamāsā anakārantā parāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ lopo ca hoti.

After other `avyayībhāva` compounds, those not ending in `a`, there is also elision of the following case endings.

Adhitthi, adhikumāri, upavadhu.

`Adhitthi`, `adhikumāri`, `upavadhu`.

Iti nāmakappe samāsakappo sattamo kaṇḍo.

Thus ends the seventh section, the chapter on compounds, in the Noun Division.

Samāsakappo niṭṭhito.

The chapter on compounds is concluded.

5. Taddhitakappa

5. Chapter on Taddhita (Derivatives)

Aṭṭhamakaṇḍa

Eighth Section

344, 361. Vāṇa’pacce[M 0.0183].

344, 361. Optionally, the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of 'descendant'.

Ṇapaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca” miccetasmiṃ atthe.

The suffix 'ṇa' is optionally used in the sense of 'his descendant'.

Vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vāsiṭṭho, vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vā, vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vāsiṭṭhī, vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vāsiṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ bhāradvājo, bhāradvājī, bhāradvājaṃ. Gotamo, gotamī, gotamaṃ. Vāsudevo, vāsudevī, vāsudevaṃ. Bāladevo, bāladevī, bāladevaṃ. Vesāmitto, vesāmittī vesāmittaṃ.

A descendant of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭho, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Vasiṭṭha'; a descendant of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭhī; a descendant of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭhaṃ. Similarly: Bhāradvājo, Bhāradvājī, Bhāradvājaṃ; Gotamo, Gotamī, Gotamaṃ; Vāsudevo, Vāsudevī, Vāsudevaṃ; Bāladevo, Bāladevī, Bāladevaṃ; Vesāmitto, Vesāmittī, Vesāmittaṃ.

345, 366. Ṇāyana ṇāna vacchādito.

345, 366. The suffixes 'ṇāyana' and 'ṇāna' from Vaccha and others.

Tasmā vacchādito gottagaṇato ṇāyanaṇānapaccayā honti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

Therefore, from the clan group beginning with Vaccha, the suffixes 'ṇāyana' and 'ṇāna' are optionally used in the sense of 'his descendant'.

Vacchassa apaccaṃvacchāyano, vacchāno, vacchassa apaccaṃ vā, vacchassa apaccaṃ vacchāyanī, vacchānī, vacchassa apaccaṃ vacchāyanaṃ, vacchānaṃ. Sakaṭassa apaccaṃ sākaṭāyano, sākaṭāno[M 0.0184], sakaṭassa apaccaṃ vā, sākaṭāyanī, sā kaṭānī, sākaṭāyanaṃ, sākaṭānaṃ. Evaṃ kaṇhāyano, kaṇhāno, kaṇhassa apaccaṃ vā. Kaṇhāyanī, kaṇhānī, kaṇhāyanaṃ, kaṇhānaṃ. Aggivessāyano, aggivessāno, aggivessāyanī, aggivessānī, aggivessāyanaṃ, aggivessānaṃ. Gacchāyano, gacchāno, gacchāyanī, gacchānī, gacchāyanaṃ, gacchānaṃ. Kappāyano, kappāno, kappāyanī, kappānī, kappāyanaṃ, kappānaṃ. Moggallāyano, moggallāno, moggallāyanī, moggallānī, moggallāyanaṃ, moggallānaṃ. Muñcāyano, muñcāno, muñcāyanī, muñcānī, muñcāyanaṃ, muñcānaṃ. Saṅghāyano, saṅghāno, saṅghāyanī, saṅghānī, saṅghāyanaṃ, saṅghānaṃ. Lomāyano, lomāno, lomāyanī, lomānī, lomāyanaṃ, lomānaṃ, sākamāyano, sākamāno, sākamāyanī, sākamānī, sākamāyanaṃ, sākamānaṃ. Nārāyano, nārāno, nārāyanī, nārānī, nārāyanaṃ, nārānaṃ. Corāyanocorāno, corāyanī, corānī, corāyanaṃ, corānaṃ, āvasālāyano, āvasālāno, āvasālāyanī, āvasālānī, āvasālāyanaṃ, āvasālānaṃ. Dvepāyano, dvepāno, dvepāyanī, dvepānī, dvepāyanaṃ, dvepānaṃ. Kuñcāyano, kuñcāno, kuñcāyanī, kuñcānī, kuñcāyanaṃ, kuñcānaṃ. Kaccāyano, kaccāno, kaccāyanī, kaccānī, kaccāyanaṃ, kaccānaṃ.

A descendant of Vaccha is Vacchāyano or Vacchāno, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Vaccha'; a descendant of Vaccha is Vacchāyanī or Vacchānī; a descendant of Vaccha is Vacchāyanaṃ or Vacchānaṃ. A descendant of Sakaṭa is Sākaṭāyano or Sākaṭāno, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Sakaṭa'; Sākaṭāyanī, Sākaṭānī; Sākaṭāyanaṃ, Sākaṭānaṃ. Similarly: Kaṇhāyano, Kaṇhāno, or 'a descendant of Kaṇha'; Kaṇhāyanī, Kaṇhānī; Kaṇhāyanaṃ, Kaṇhānaṃ. Aggivessāyano, Aggivessāno; Aggivessāyanī, Aggivessānī; Aggivessāyanaṃ, Aggivessānaṃ. Gacchāyano, Gacchāno; Gacchāyanī, Gacchānī; Gacchāyanaṃ, Gacchānaṃ. Kappāyano, Kappāno; Kappāyanī, Kappānī; Kappāyanaṃ, Kappānaṃ. Moggallāyano, Moggallāno; Moggallāyanī, Moggallānī; Moggallāyanaṃ, Moggallānaṃ. Muñcāyano, Muñcāno; Muñcāyanī, Muñcānī; Muñcāyanaṃ, Muñcānaṃ. Saṅghāyano, Saṅghāno; Saṅghāyanī, Saṅghānī; Saṅghāyanaṃ, Saṅghānaṃ. Lomāyano, Lomāno; Lomāyanī, Lomānī; Lomāyanaṃ, Lomānaṃ. Sākamāyano, Sākamāno; Sākamāyanī, Sākamānī; Sākamāyanaṃ, Sākamānaṃ. Nārāyano, Nārāno; Nārāyanī, Nārānī; Nārāyanaṃ, Nārānaṃ. Corāyano, Corāno; Corāyanī, Corānī; Corāyanaṃ, Corānaṃ. Āvasālāyano, Āvasālāno; Āvasālāyanī, Āvasālānī; Āvasālāyanaṃ, Āvasālānaṃ. Dvepāyano, Dvepāno; Dvepāyanī, Dvepānī; Dvepāyanaṃ, Dvepānaṃ. Kuñcāyano, Kuñcāno; Kuñcāyanī, Kuñcānī; Kuñcāyanaṃ, Kuñcānaṃ. Kaccāyano, Kaccāno; Kaccāyanī, Kaccānī; Kaccāyanaṃ, Kaccānaṃ.

346, 367. Ṇeyyo [M 0.0185] kattikādīhi.

346, 367. The suffix 'ṇeyya' from Kattikā and others.

Tehi gottagaṇehi kattikādīhi ṇeyyapaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

From those clan groups beginning with Kattikā, the suffix 'ṇeyya' is optionally used in the sense of 'his descendant'.

Kattikāya apaccaṃ kattikeyyo, kattikāya apaccaṃ vā. Evaṃ venateyyo, rohiṇeyyo, gaṅgeyyo, kaddameyyo, nādeyyo, āleyyo, āheyo, kāmeyyo, suciyā apaccaṃ soceyyo, sāleyyo, bāleyyo, māleyyo, kāleyyo.

A descendant of Kattikā is Kattikeyyo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Kattikā'. Similarly: Venateyyo, Rohiṇeyyo, Gaṅgeyyo, Kaddameyyo, Nādeyyo, Āleyyo, Āheyo, Kāmeyyo. A descendant of Suci is Soceyyo; Sāleyyo, Bāleyyo, Māleyyo, Kāleyyo.

347, 368. Ato ṇi vā.

347, 368. Optionally, the suffix 'ṇi' from 'a'-ending stems.

Tasmā akārato ṇipaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

Therefore, from 'a'-ending stems, the suffix 'ṇi' is optionally used in the sense of 'his descendant'.

Dakkhassa apaccaṃ dakkhi, dakkhassa apaccaṃ vā. Duṇassa apaccaṃ doṇi, duṇassa apaccaṃ vā, evaṃ vāsavi, sakyaputti, nāṭaputti, dāsaputti, dāsavi, vāruṇi, gaṇḍi, bāladevi, pāvaki, jenadatti, buddhi, dhammi, saṅghi, kappi, anuruddhi.

A descendant of Dakkha is Dakkhi, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Dakkha'. A descendant of Duṇa is Doṇi, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Duṇa'. Similarly: Vāsavi, Sakyaputti, Nāṭaputti, Dāsaputti, Dāsavi, Vāruṇi, Gaṇḍi, Bāladevi, Pāvaki, Jenadatti, Buddhi, Dhammi, Saṅghi, Kappi, Anuruddhi.

Vāti vikappanatthena ṇikapaccayo hoti “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe. Sakyaputtassa apaccaṃ sakyaputtiko. Evaṃ nāṭaputtiko, jenadattiko.

By the word 'vā', which indicates an alternative, the suffix 'ṇika' is also used in the sense of 'his descendant'. A descendant of Sakyaputta is Sakyaputtiko. Similarly: Nāṭaputtiko, Jenadattiko.

148, 371. Ṇavo’ [M 0.0186] pakvādīhi.

348, 371. The suffix 'ṇava' from Upaku and others.

Upakuiccevamādīhi ṇavapaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

From Upaku and others, the suffix 'ṇava' is optionally used in the sense of 'his descendant'.

Upakussa apaccaṃ opakavo, upakussa apaccaṃ vā. Manuno apaccaṃ mānavo, manuno apaccaṃ vā. Bhaggussa apaccaṃ bhaggavo, bhaggussa apaccaṃ vā, paṇḍussa apaccaṃ paṇḍavo, paṇḍussa apaccaṃ vā, bahussa apaccaṃ bāhavo, bahussa apaccaṃ vā.

A descendant of Upaku is Opakavo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Upaku'. A descendant of Manu is Mānavo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Manu'. A descendant of Bhaggu is Bhaggavo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Bhaggu'. A descendant of Paṇḍu is Paṇḍavo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Paṇḍu'. A descendant of Bahu is Bāhavo, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of Bahu'.

349, 372. Ṇera vidhavādito.

349, 372. The suffix 'ṇera' from Vidhavā and others.

Tasmā vidhavādito ṇerapaccayo hoti vā “tassāpacca”miccetasmiṃ atthe.

Therefore, from Vidhavā and others, the suffix 'ṇera' is optionally used in the sense of 'his/her descendant'.

Vidhavāya apaccaṃ vedhavero, vidhavāya apaccaṃ vā. Bandhukiyā apaccaṃ bandhukero, bandhukiyā apaccaṃ vā. Samaṇassa apaccaṃ sāmaṇero, samaṇassa apaccaṃ vā. Evaṃ sāmaṇerī, sāmaṇeraṃ, nāḷikero, nāḷikerī, nāḷikeraṃ.

A descendant of a widow (vidhavā) is Vedhavero, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of a widow'. A descendant of an unchaste woman (bandhukī) is Bandhukero, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of an unchaste woman'. A descendant of a recluse (samaṇa) is Sāmaṇero, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'a descendant of a recluse'. Similarly: Sāmaṇerī, Sāmaṇeraṃ; Nāḷikero, Nāḷikerī, Nāḷikeraṃ.

350, 373. Yena vā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ tarati carati vahati ṇiko.

350, 373. The suffix 'ṇika' is optionally used in the senses of 'mixed with that', 'crosses by that', 'travels by that', and 'carries by that'.

Yena vā saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, yena vā tarati, yena vā carati, yena vā vahati iccetesvatthesu ṇikapaccayo hoti vā.

The suffix 'ṇika' is optionally used in these senses: 'that with which it is mixed', 'that by which one crosses', 'that by which one travels', and 'that by which one carries'.

Tilena [M 0.0187] saṃsaṭṭhaṃ bhojanaṃ telikaṃ, tilena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ vā. Evaṃ goḷikaṃ, ghātikaṃ.

Food mixed with sesame (tila) is Telikaṃ, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'mixed with sesame'. Similarly: Goḷikaṃ (mixed with molasses), Ghātikaṃ (mixed with ghee).

Nāvāya taratīti nāviko, nāvāya tarati vā. Evaṃ oḷumpiko.

One who crosses by boat (nāvā) is a Nāviko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who crosses by boat'. Similarly: Oḷumpiko (one who crosses by raft).

Sakaṭena caratīti sākaṭiko, sakaṭena carati vā. Evaṃ pattiko, daṇḍiko, dhammiko, pādiko.

One who travels by cart (sakaṭa) is a Sākaṭiko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who travels by cart'. Similarly: Pattiko (one who travels with a bowl), Daṇḍiko (one who travels with a staff), Dhammiko (one who lives righteously), Pādiko (one who travels on foot).

Sīsena vahatīti sīsiko, sīsena vahati vā. Aṃsena vahatīti aṃsiko, aṃsena vahati vā. Evaṃ khandhiko, aṅguliko.

One who carries with the head (sīsa) is a Sīsiko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who carries with the head'. One who carries with the shoulder (aṃsa) is an Aṃsiko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who carries with the shoulder'. Similarly: Khandhiko (one who carries on the shoulder), Aṅguliko (one who carries with the finger).

Vāti vikappanatthena aññesupi ṇikapaccayo hoti. Rājagahe vasatīti rājagahiko, rājagahe vasati vā. Rājagahe jāto rājagahiko, rājagahe jāto vā. Evaṃ māgadhiko, sāvatthiko, kāpila vatthiko, pāṭaliputtiko, vesāliko.

By the word 'vā', which indicates an alternative, the suffix 'ṇika' is also used in other senses. One who dwells in Rājagaha is a Rājagahiko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who dwells in Rājagaha'. One who is born in Rājagaha is a Rājagahiko, or [alternatively, the phrase] 'one who is born in Rājagaha'. Similarly: Māgadhiko, Sāvatthiko, Kāpilavatthiko, Pāṭaliputtiko, Vesāliko.

351, 374. Tamadhīte tenakatādi sannidhāna niyoga sippa bhaṇḍa jīvikatthesu ca.

351, 374. And in the senses of: that which is studied, that which is done by it and so forth, that which is present in it, that to which one is appointed, that which is one's craft, that which is one's merchandise, and that which is one's livelihood.

Tamadhīte, tenakatādiatthe, tamhi sannidhānā, tattha niyutto, tamassa sippaṃ, tamassa bhaṇḍaṃ, tamassa jīvikaṃ iccetesvatthesu ca ṇikapaccayo hoti vā.

The suffix ṇika optionally occurs in these senses: 'he studies that'; 'done by that,' and so forth; 'present in that'; 'appointed thereto'; 'that is his craft'; 'that is his merchandise'; and 'that is his livelihood'.

Vinayamadhīte [M 0.0188] venayiko, vinayamadhīte vā. Evaṃ suttantiko, ābhidhammiko, veyyākaraṇiko.

He who studies the Vinaya is a Venayika; or, one who studies the Vinaya. Similarly, a Suttantika, an Ābhidhammika, a Veyyākaraṇika.

Kāyena kataṃ kammaṃ kāyikaṃ, kāyena kataṃ kammaṃ vā. Evaṃ vācasikaṃ, mānasikaṃ.

An action done by the body is a bodily action (kāyikaṃ); or, an action done by the body. Similarly, a verbal action (vācasikaṃ) and a mental action (mānasikaṃ).
