617, 633. Na ma ka rānamantānaṃ niyuttatamhi.

617, 633. For roots ending in 'n', 'm', 'k', and 'r', there is no elision when the 'ta' suffix joined with 'i' follows.

Nakāra makāra kakāra rakārānaṃ dhātvantānaṃ lopo na hoti ikārayutte tapaccaye pare.

For roots ending in the letters 'n', 'm', 'k', and 'r', there is no elision of the final letter when the 'ta' suffix joined with the letter 'i' follows.

Hanibhuṃ, gamito, ramito, sakito, sarito, karitvā.

Hanibhuṃ, gamito, ramito, sakito, sarito, karitvā.

Iyuttatamhīti kimatthaṃ? Gato, sato.

Why 'when joined with i'? Gato, sato.

618, 571. Na ka gattaṃ ca jāṇvumhi.

618, 571. 'Ca' and 'ja' do not become 'ka' and 'ga' before 'ṇvu'.

Cakāra jakārā kakāra gakārattaṃ nāpajjante ṇvumhi paccaye pare.

The letters 'c' and 'j' do not become 'k' and 'g' respectively when the suffix 'ṇvu' follows.

Pacatīti pācako, yajatīti yājako.

Pacatīti pācako, yajatīti yājako.

619, 573. Karassa [M 0.0286] ca tattaṃ tusmiṃ.

619, 573. And for 'kar', there is substitution by 't' before 'tu'.

Karaiccetassa dhātussa antassa rakārassa takārattaṃ hoti tupaccaye pare.

For this root 'kar', its final letter 'r' becomes 't' when the suffix 'tu' follows.

Karotīti kattā, karontīti kattāro.

Karotīti kattā, karontīti kattāro.

620, 549. Tuṃ tuna tabbesu vā.

620, 549. Optionally before 'tuṃ', 'tuna', and 'tabba'.

Karaiccetassa dhātussa antassa rakārassa takārattaṃ hoti vā tuṃ tuna tabbaiccetesu paccayesu.

For this root 'kar', its final letter 'r' optionally becomes 't' before these suffixes: 'tuṃ', 'tuna', and 'tabba'.

Kattuṃ, kātuṃ, kattuna. Kātuna, kattabbaṃ, kātabbaṃ.

Kattuṃ, kātuṃ, kattuna, kātuna, kattabbaṃ, kātabbaṃ.

621, 553. Kāritaṃ viya ṇānubandho.

621, 553. A suffix with 'ṇ' as an anubandha is like a causative.

Ṇakārānubandho paccayo kāritaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo vā.

A suffix with the letter 'ṇ' as an anubandha should optionally be regarded as a causative.

Dāho, deho, vāho, bāho, cāgo, vāro, cāro, parikkhāro, dāyako, nāyako, lāvako, bhāvako, kārī, ghātī, dāyī.

Dāho, deho, vāho, bāho, cāgo, vāro, cāro, parikkhāro, dāyako, nāyako, lāvako, bhāvako, kārī, ghātī, dāyī.

Vāti kimatthaṃ? Upakkharo.

Why 'vā'? Upakkharo.

622, 570. Anakā [M 0.0287] yu ṇvūnaṃ.

622, 570. Ana and aka for yu and ṇvu.

Yuṇvuiccetesaṃ paccayānaṃ ana akaiccete ādesā honti.

For the suffixes yu and ṇvu, the substitutions ana and aka occur.

Nandanaṃ, kārako.

Nandanaṃ, kārako.

623, 554. Ka gā ca jānaṃ.

623, 554. Ka and ga for ca and ja.

Ca jaiccetesaṃ dhātvantānaṃ kakāragakārādesā honti ṇānubandhe paccaye pare.

For roots ending in ca and ja, the substitutions ka and ga occur when a suffix with ṇ as an anubandha follows.

Pāko, yogo.

Pāko, yogo.

Iti kibbidhānakappe pañcamo kaṇḍo.

Thus ends the Fifth Section in the Chapter on Kvi Suffixes.

Kitakappo niṭṭhito.

The Chapter on Kita Suffixes is completed.

8. Uṇādikappa

8. The Chapter on Uṇādi Suffixes

Chaṭṭhakaṇḍa

Sixth Section

624, 563. Kattari [M 0.0288] kita.

624, 563. The kita suffixes are used in the agentive sense.

Kattuiccetasmiṃ atthe kita paccayā honti.

In the sense of an agent, the kita suffixes occur.

Kāru, kāruko, kārako, pācako, kattā, janitā, pacitā, netā.

Kāru, kāruko, kārako, pācako, kattā, janitā, pacitā, netā.

625, 605. Bhāvakammesu kiccatta khatthā.

625, 605. In the senses of state and object, the kicca, tta, and khattha suffixes.

Bhāvakammaiccetesvatthesu kicca tta khatthaiccete paccayā honti.

In the senses of state (bhāva) and object (kamma), the suffixes kicca, tta, and khattha occur.

Upasampādetabbaṃ upasampādanīyaṃ bhavatā, sayitabbaṃ bhavatā, kattabbaṃ bhavatā, bhottabbo odano bhavatā, asitabbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā, asitaṃ bhavatā, sayitaṃ bhavatā, pacitaṃ bhavatā, asitaṃ asanaṃ bhavatā, sayitaṃ sayanaṃ bhavatā, pacito odano bhavatā, kiñcissayo, īsassayo, dussayo, sussayo bhavatā.

Ordination should be conferred by you; it should be slept by you; it should be done by you; rice should be eaten by you; food should be eaten by you; it has been eaten by you; it has been slept by you; it has been cooked by you; eating has been done by you; sleeping has been done by you; rice has been cooked by you; [a bed that is] difficult to lie on, easy to lie on, difficult to lie on, and easy to lie on by you.

626, 634. Kammani [M 0.0289] dutiyāya tto.

626, 634. The suffix ta is used in the sense of the object, with the agent in the accusative.

Kammani iccetasmiṃ atthe dutiyāyaṃ vibhattiyaṃ kattari ttapaccayo hoti.

In the sense of the object, the suffix tta occurs when the agent is in the accusative case.

Dānaṃ dinno devadatto, sīlaṃ rakkhito devadatto, bhattaṃ bhutto devadatto, garuṃ upāsito devadatto.

Devadatta has given a gift; Devadatta has guarded morality; Devadatta has eaten food; Devadatta has attended upon the teacher.

627, 652. Khyādīhi māna ma ca to vā.

627, 652. From roots such as khi, the suffixes māna and ma occur, and ma optionally becomes ta.

Khi bhī su ru hu vā dhū hi lū pī adaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi mana paccayo hoti, massa ca to hoti vā.

From roots such as khi, bhī, su, ru, hu, vā, dhū, hi, lū, pī, and ada, the suffix mana occurs, and its ma optionally becomes ta.

Khīyanti upaddavā etthāti khemo, bhāyitabboti bhemo, bhāyanti etasmāti vā bhemo, raṃsiyo abhissavetīti somo, ravati gacchatīti romo, huvati juhvati etenāti homo, paṭilomavasena vāti gacchatīti vāmo, lāmakavasena vāti gacchati pavattatīti vā vāmo, dhunāti kampatīti dhūmo, seṭṭhabhāvena hinoti pavattati cittaṃ etasminti hemo, lunitabboti lomo, maṃsacammāni lunāti chindatīti vā lomo, piyanaṃ pemo, piyāyitabboti vā pemo, sukhadukkhaṃ adati bhakkhatīti attā, jātijarāmaraṇādīhi adīyate bhakkhīyateti vā attā, ātumā.

Dangers are destroyed here, thus it is safety (khemo). It is to be feared, thus it is fearful (bhemo); or they fear from this, thus it is fearful (bhemo). It pours forth rays, thus it is the moon (somo). It sounds or goes, thus it is body hair (romo). One offers or sacrifices with this, thus it is an oblation (homo). It goes against the grain, thus it is left (vāmo); or it proceeds in a base manner, thus it is left or base (vāmo). It shakes or trembles, thus it is smoke (dhūmo). The mind proceeds from this in a superior way, thus it is gold (hemo). It is to be cut, thus it is body hair (lomo); or it cuts or severs flesh and skin, thus it is body hair (lomo). Loving is love (pemo); or it is to be loved, thus it is love (pemo). It eats or consumes pleasure and pain, thus it is the self (attā); or it is eaten or consumed by birth, aging, death, and so on, thus it is the self (attā); ātumā.

628, 653. Samādīhi [M 0.0290] tha mā.

628, 653. From roots such as sam, the suffixes tha and ma.

Samu damu dara raha du hi si bhī dā yā sā ṭhābhasaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi tha ma paccayā honti.

From roots such as samu, damu, dara, raha, du, hi, si, bhī, dā, yā, sā, ṭhā, and bhasa, the suffixes tha and ma occur.

Sametīti samatho, damatīti damatho, damanaṃ vā damatho, damitabboti vā damatho, daratīti daratho, jiṇṇabhāvaṃ rahissati gaṇhissatīti ratho, dabbasambhāre rahati gaṇhātīti vā ratho, davati gacchatīti dumo, davati vuddhi viruḷhi gacchati pavattatīti uddhaṃ vā dumo, pathavīpabbatādīsu gacchati patatīti himo, kammavācāya bandhati etthāti sīmā. Bandhitabbāti vā sīmā. Bhāyanti etasmāti bhīmo, satte avakhaṇḍenti nivārenti etenāti dāmo, mūsikādīhi khādīyati avakhaṇḍīyatīti vā dāmo, yāti gacchatīti yāmo, paresaṃ cittaṃ gaṇhituṃ samatthetīti sāmo, tiṭṭhanti etenāti thāmo, bhasati bhasmīkarīyatīti bhasmā.

He is calm, thus it is calm (samatho). He tames, thus it is taming (damatho); or taming is damatho; or it is to be tamed, thus it is damatho. He fears, thus it is fear (daratho). It will leave behind or take the state of being old, thus it is a chariot (ratho); or it takes materials, thus it is a chariot (ratho). It goes, thus it is a tree (dumo); or it goes upwards, grows, sprouts, and proceeds, thus it is a tree (dumo). It goes or falls on the earth, mountains, etc., thus it is snow (himo). One binds here with a formal act, thus it is a boundary (sīmā); or it is to be bound, thus it is a boundary (sīmā). They fear from this, thus it is fearful (bhīmo). With this they cut off or restrain beings, thus it is a rope (dāmo); or it is eaten or cut by mice, etc., thus it is a rope (dāmo). It goes, thus it is a watch (yāmo). It is able to capture the minds of others, thus it is conciliation (sāmo). They stand by this, thus it is strength (thāmo). It is consumed by fire or reduced to ashes, thus it is ashes (bhasmā).

629, 569. Gahassu’padhasse vā.

629, 569. For the penultimate vowel of gah, optionally e.

Gahaiccetassa dhātussa upadhassa akārassa etta hoti vā.

For the penultimate vowel a of this root gah, e optionally occurs.

Dabbasambhāra gaṇhātīti gehaṃ, gahaṃ.

It takes materials, thus it is a house (gehaṃ, gahaṃ).

630, 654. Masussa [M 0.0291] sussa cchara ccherā.

630, 654. For the s of masu, cchara and cchera.

Masuiccetassa pāṭipadikassa sussa ccharaccherādesā honti.

For the s of this nominal stem masu, the substitutions cchara and cchera occur.

Maccharatīti maccharo, evaṃ macchero.

One is miserly, thus a miser (maccharo); similarly, macchero.

631, 655. Āpubbacarassa ca.

631, 655. And of the root 'car' preceded by 'ā'.

Āpubbassa caraiccetassa dhātussa cchariyaccharaccherā desā honti, āpubbassa ca rasso hoti.

For this root 'car' preceded by 'ā', the substitutes 'cchariya', 'cchara', and 'cchera' occur, and the preceding 'ā' is shortened.

Ābhuso caritabbanti acchariyaṃ. Evaṃ accharaṃ, accheraṃ.

It is to be practiced exceedingly, thus it is wonderful (acchariyaṃ). Similarly, accharaṃ, accheraṃ.

Caggahaṇena masussa sussāpi cchariyādeso hoti, macchariyaṃ.

By the inclusion of 'ca', the substitute 'cchariya' also occurs for the 's' of 'masu', forming 'macchariyaṃ' (miserliness).

632, 656. Ala kala salehi layā.

632, 656. After the roots ala, kala, and sala, the suffixes are la and ya.

Ala kala salaiccetehi dhātūhi la yapaccayā honti.

From these roots, ala, kala, and sala, the suffixes la and ya occur.

Alati samatthetīti allaṃ, kalitabbaṃ saṅkhyātabbanti kallaṃ, salati gacchati pavisatīti sallaṃ. Evaṃ alyaṃ, kalyaṃ, salyaṃ.

One is capable, thus it is wet (allaṃ). It is to be calculated, to be reckoned, thus it is fit (kallaṃ). It moves, goes, enters, thus it is a dart (sallaṃ). Similarly: alyaṃ, kalyaṃ, salyaṃ.

633, 657. Yāṇa [M 0.0292] lāṇā.

633, 657. Yāṇa and lāṇa are the suffixes.

Tehi kala salaiccetehi dhātūhi yāṇa lāṇapaccayā honti.

From those roots, kala and sala, the suffixes yāṇa and lāṇa occur.

Kalitabbaṃ saṅkhyātabbanti kalyāṇaṃ, gaṇato paṭikkamitvā salanti etthāti paṭisalyāṇaṃ. Evaṃ sallāṇo, paṭisallāṇo.

It is to be calculated, to be reckoned, thus it is good (kalyāṇaṃ). Having retreated from the group, they dwell here, thus it is solitude (paṭisalyāṇaṃ). Similarly, sallāṇo, paṭisallāṇo.

634, 658. Mathissa thassa lo ca.

634, 658. And for the 'th' of the root 'math', 'l' is the substitute.

Mathaiccetassa dhātussa thassa lādesohoti. Aññamaññaṃ mathati viloḷatīti mallo, mallaṃ.

For the 'th' of this root 'math', 'l' is the substitute. One who agitates or churns another is a wrestler (mallo); or it is wrestling (mallaṃ).

Caggahaṇena lato ko ca āgamo hoti. Mallako, mallakaṃ.

By the inclusion of 'ca', the augment 'ka' also occurs after 'la', forming: mallako, mallakaṃ.

635, 559. Pesātisaggapattakālesukiccā.

635, 559. In the senses of command, permission, and fitness of time, the kicca suffixes occur.

Pesa atisagga pattakālaiccetesvatthesu kiccapaccayā honti.

In these senses—command, permission, and fitness of time—the kicca suffixes occur.

Kattabbaṃ kammaṃ bhavatā, karaṇīyaṃ kiccaṃ bhavatā, bhottabbaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā, bhojanīyaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavatā, ajjhayitabbaṃ ajjheyyaṃ bhavatā, ajjhayanīyaṃ ajjheyyaṃ bhavatā.

Work is to be done by you; a task is to be done by you; food is to be eaten by you; a meal is to be eaten by you; a text is to be studied by you; a text is to be studied by you.

636, 659. Avassakā’dhamiṇesu [M 0.0293] ṇī ca.

636, 659. In the senses of necessity and being a debtor, the suffix ṇī also occurs.

Avassaka adhamiṇaiccetesvatthesu ṇīpaccayo hoti, kiccā ca.

In these senses of necessity and being a debtor, the suffix ṇī occurs, and also the kicca suffixes.

Avassate tāva – kārīsi me kammaṃ avassaṃ hārīsi me bhāraṃ avassaṃ.

Firstly, in the sense of necessity: You must certainly do my work; you must certainly carry my burden.

Adhamiṇe – dāyīsi me sataṃ iṇaṃ, dhārīsi me sahassaṃ iṇaṃ.

In the sense of being a debtor: You shall give me a hundred as a debt; you shall owe me a thousand as a debt.

Kiccā ca – dātabbaṃ me bhavatā sataṃ iṇaṃ. Dhārayitabbaṃ me bhavatā sahassaṃ iṇaṃ, kattabbaṃ me bhavatā gehaṃ, karaṇīyaṃ me bhavatā kiccaṃ, kāriyaṃ me bhavatā sayanaṃ.

And with the kicca suffixes: A hundred is to be given to me by you as a debt. A thousand is to be owed to me by you as a debt. A house is to be made for me by you. A task is to be done for me by you. A bed is to be made for me by you.

637, 0. Arahasakkādīhi tuṃ.

637, 0. With words such as araha, sakka, and so on, tuṃ is used.

Araha sakka bhabbaiccevamādīhi payoge sati sabbadhātūhi tuṃpaccayo hoti.

When there is usage with such words as araha, sakka, bhabba, and so on, the suffix tuṃ occurs after all roots.

Arahā bhavaṃ vattuṃ, arahā bhavaṃ kattuṃ, sakkā bhavaṃ hantuṃ, sakkā bhavaṃ janetuṃ, janituṃ, bhavituṃ, sakkā bhavaṃ dātuṃ, sakkā bhavaṃ gantuṃ, tabbo bhavaṃ janetuṃ iccevamādi.

The venerable one is worthy to speak; the venerable one is worthy to do; the venerable one is able to destroy; the venerable one is able to generate, to beget, or to become; the venerable one is able to give; the venerable one is able to go; the venerable one is fit to generate; and so on.

638, 660. Vajādīhipabbajjādayo [M 0.0294] nippajjante.

638, 660. From the root vaja and others, words such as pabbajjā and others are irregularly formed.

Vajaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, upasaggapaccayādīhi ca pabbajjādayo saddā nippajjante.

From roots such as vaja and so on, and by means of prefixes, suffixes, and so on, words such as pabbajjā and others are irregularly formed.

Paṭhamameva vajitabbāti pabbajjā, iñjanaṃ ejjā, samajjanaṃ samajjā, nisīdanaṃ nisajjā, vijānanaṃ vijjā visajjanaṃ visajjā, padanaṃ pajjā, hananaṃ vajjhā, esanaṃ icchā, atiesanaṃ aticchā, sadanaṃ sajjā, sayanti etthāti seyyā, sammā cittaṃ nidheti etāyāti saddhā, caritabbā cariyā, karaṇaṃ kiriyā, rujanaṃ rucchā, padanaṃ pacchā, riñcanaṃ ricchā, tikicchanaṃ titicchā, saṃkocanaṃ saṃkucchā, madanaṃ macchā, labhanaṃ lacchā, radihabbāti racchā, radanaṃ vilekhanaṃ vāracchā, adho bhāgena gacchatīti tiracchā, tiracchāno, ajanaṃ acchā, titikkhatīti titikkhā, saha āgamanaṃ sāgacchā, duṭṭhu bhakkhanaṃ dobhacchā, duṭṭhu rosanaṃ durucchā, pucchanaṃ pucchā, muhanaṃ mucchā, vasanaṃ vacchā, kacanaṃ kacchā, saha kathanaṃ sākacchā, tudanaṃ tucchā, visanaṃ vicchā, pisanaṃ picchillā, sukhadukkhaṃ mudati bhakkhatīti maccho[M 0.0295], sattānaṃ pāṇaṃ museti cajetīti maccu, satanaṃ saccaṃ, uddhaṃ dhunāti kampatīti uddhaccaṃ, naṭanaṃ naccaṃ, nitanaṃ niccaṃ, tathanaṃ tacchaṃ iccevamādi.

That which is to be gone forth to in the first place is renunciation; stirring is agitation; assembling is an assembly; sitting is sitting down; knowing is knowledge; sending forth is dismissal; going is a path; killing is what is punishable; seeking is desire; excessive seeking is excessive desire; sinking is readiness; they lie here, thus it is a bed; by this, one rightly places the mind, thus it is faith; that which is to be practiced is practice; doing is action; ailing is dislike; going is behind; abandoning is leaving; curing is endurance; contracting is shrinking; intoxicating is a fish; obtaining is what is obtained; that which is to be dug is a road; cutting or carving is vāracchā; it goes horizontally, thus it is an animal; going is a bear; one endures, thus it is endurance; coming together is conversation; bad eating is famine; harsh anger is ill-will; asking is a question; fainting is infatuation; dwelling is a calf; binding is a loincloth; speaking together is discussion; piercing is emptiness; entering is scattering; grinding is slime; it delights in pleasure and pain, thus it is a fish; it steals the life of beings or makes them abandon it, thus it is death; being is truth; it shakes upwards, thus it is restlessness; dancing is dance; leading is permanence; being so is reality; and so on.

639, 585. Kvilopo ca.

639, 585. And the elision of the suffix kvi.

Kvilopo hoti, puna ca nippajjante.

The elision of the suffix kvi occurs, and they are also formed in this way.

Vividhehi sīlādiguṇehi bhavatīti vibhū, visesena vā bhavatīti vibhū, sayaṃ attanā bhavatīti sayambhū, abhivitvā bhavatīti abhibhū, saṃ suṭṭhu dhunāti kampatīti sandhū, visesena bhāti dibbatīti vibhā, nissesena bhāti dibbatīti nibhā, pakārena bhāti dibbatīti pabhā, saha bhāsanti etthāti sabhā, ābhuso bhāti dibbatīti ābhā, bhujena kuṭilena gacchatīti bhujago, turitaturito gacchatīti turago, saṃ suṭṭhu pathaviṃ khanatīti saṅkho, visesena yamati uparamatīti viyo, suṭṭhu manati jānātīti sumo, pari samantato tanoti vitthāretīti parito iccevamādi.

One who exists with various virtues such as morality, thus is 'vibhū'; or one who exists in a special way, thus is 'vibhū'; one who exists by oneself, thus is 'sayambhū'; one who exists having overcome, thus is 'abhibhū'; one who thoroughly shakes or trembles, thus is 'sandhū'; it shines or plays in a special way, thus is 'vibhā'; it shines or plays without remainder, thus is 'nibhā'; it shines or plays in a particular manner, thus is 'pabhā'; where they speak together, thus is 'sabhā'; it shines or plays exceedingly, thus is 'ābhā'; it goes with a crooked limb, thus is 'bhujago'; it goes very swiftly, thus is 'turago'; it thoroughly digs the earth, thus is 'saṅkho'; it especially restrains or ceases, thus is 'viyo'; one who knows well, thus is 'sumo'; it spreads or extends all around, thus is 'parito'; and so forth.

640, 0. Sacajānaṃ kagā ṇānubandhe.

For roots ending in 'c' and 'j', 'k' and 'g' are the substitutes when a suffix with the marker 'ṇa' follows.

Saca jānaṃ dhātūnamantānaṃ cajānaṃ kagādesā honti yathāsaṅkhyaṃ ṇānubandhe paccaye pare.

For the final 'c' and 'j' of roots, 'k' and 'g' are the respective substitutes when a suffix with 'ṇa' as an indicatory letter follows.

Oko[M 0.0296], pāko, seko, soko, viveko, cāgo, yogo, bhogo, rogo, rāgo, bhāgo, bhaṅgo, raṅgo, saṅgo.

Oko (abode), pāko (ripening), seko (sprinkling), soko (sorrow), viveko (seclusion), cāgo (generosity), yogo (application), bhogo (enjoyment), rogo (disease), rāgo (passion), bhāgo (portion), bhaṅgo (breaking), raṅgo (color), saṅgo (attachment).

641, 572. Nudādīhi yuṇvūnamanānanākānanakā sakāritehi ca.

From 'nud' and other roots, and from causatives, for 'yu' and 'ṇvu', 'ana', 'ānana', 'aka', and 'ānanaka' are the substitutes.

Nuda sūda jana su lū hu pu bhū ñā a sa samuiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, phanda citi āṇa iccevamādīhi sakāritehi ca yuṇvūnaṃ paccayānaṃ ana ānana aka ānanakādesā honti yathāsaṅkhyaṃ kattari, bhāvakaraṇesu ca.

From the roots `nud`, `sūd`, `jana`, `su`, `lū`, `hu`, `pu`, `bhū`, `ñā`, `a`, `sa`, `samu`, and so forth, and from causatives like `phanda`, `citi`, `āṇa`, and so forth, for the suffixes `yu` and `ṇvu`, the respective substitutes are `ana`, `ānana`, `aka`, and `ānanaka`, in the agent sense, and in the abstract and instrumental senses.

Kattari tāva – panudatīti panūdano. Evaṃ sūdano, janano, savaṇo, lavano, havano, pavano, bhavano, ñāṇo, asano, samaṇo.

Firstly, in the agent sense: one who dispels, thus is 'panūdano'. Similarly, 'sūdano' (one who destroys), 'janano' (one who produces), 'savaṇo' (one who hears), 'lavano' (one who reaps), 'havano' (one who sacrifices), 'pavano' (one who purifies), 'bhavano' (one who exists), 'ñāṇo' (one who knows), 'asano' (one who eats), 'samaṇo' (one who is tranquil).

Bhāve ca – panudate panūdanaṃ. Evaṃ sūdanaṃ, jananaṃ, savaṇaṃ, lavanaṃ, havanaṃ, pavanaṃ, bhavanaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, asanaṃ, samaṇaṃ, sañjānanaṃ, kuyate kānanaṃ.

And in the abstract sense: the act of dispelling is 'panūdanaṃ'. Similarly, 'sūdanaṃ' (destroying), 'jananaṃ' (producing), 'savaṇaṃ' (hearing), 'lavanaṃ' (reaping), 'havanaṃ' (sacrificing), 'pavanaṃ' (purifying), 'bhavanaṃ' (being), 'ñāṇaṃ' (knowing), 'asanaṃ' (eating), 'samaṇaṃ' (tranquility), 'sañjānanaṃ' (perceiving); it is made, thus 'kānanaṃ' (forest).

Kārite ca – phandāpīyate phandāpanaṃ, cetāpīyate cetāpanaṃ, āṇāpīyate āṇāpanaṃ.

And in the causative sense: it is caused to tremble, thus 'phandāpanaṃ' (causing to tremble); it is caused to think, thus 'cetāpanaṃ' (causing to think); it is caused to be commanded, thus 'āṇāpanaṃ' (causing to be commanded).

Karaṇe – nudanti anenāti nūdanaṃ, evaṃ sūdanaṃ, jananaṃ, savaṇaṃ, lavaṇaṃ, havanaṃ, pavanaṃ, bhaganaṃ, ñāṇaṃ, asanaṃ, savaṇaṃ.

In the instrumental sense: they push with this, thus 'nūdanaṃ' (instrument for pushing). Similarly, 'sūdanaṃ' (instrument for destroying), 'jananaṃ' (instrument for producing), 'savaṇaṃ' (instrument for hearing), 'lavaṇaṃ' (instrument for reaping), 'havanaṃ' (instrument for sacrificing), 'pavanaṃ' (instrument for purifying), 'bhaganaṃ' (instrument for breaking), 'ñāṇaṃ' (instrument for knowing), 'asanaṃ' (instrument for eating), 'savaṇaṃ' (instrument for hearing).

Puna [M 0.0297] kattari – nudatīti nūdako, sūdatīti sūdadhakā, janetīti janako, suṇotīti sāvako, lunātīti lāvako, juhotīti hāvako, punātīti pāvako, bhavatīti bhāvako, jānātīti jānako, asatīti asako, upāsatīti upāsako, sametīti samako.

Again, in the agent sense: one who pushes, thus is 'nūdako'; one who cooks, thus is 'sūdako'; one who begets, thus is 'janako'; one who hears, thus is 'sāvako'; one who reaps, thus is 'lāvako'; one who offers, thus is 'hāvako'; one who purifies, thus is 'pāvako'; one who becomes, thus is 'bhāvako'; one who knows, thus is 'jānako'; one who eats, thus is 'asako'; one who attends, thus is 'upāsako'; one who is tranquil, thus is 'samako'.

Kārite tu – phandāpayatīti phandāpayako. Evaṃ āṇāpayako, cetāpayako, sañjānanako.

In the causative sense, however: one who causes to tremble, thus is 'phandāpayako'. Similarly, 'āṇāpayako' (one who causes to command), 'cetāpayako' (one who causes to think), 'sañjānanako' (one who causes to perceive).

642, 588. I ya ta ma ki e sāna’mantassaro dīghaṃ kvaci du sa ssa guṇaṃ do raṃ sakkhī ca.

For 'i', 'ya', 'ta', 'ma', 'ki', 'e', and 'sa', the final vowel is lengthened; sometimes for 'dus', there is guṇa, 'd' becomes 'r', and 's' becomes 'sa', 'kkha', or 'ī'.

Iya ta ma ki e saiccetesaṃ sabbanāmānamanto saro dīghamāpajjate, kvaci dusaiccetassa dhātussa ukāro guṇamāpajjate, dakāro rakāramāpajjate, dhātvantassa sassa ca sa kkha īiccete ādesā honti yathāsambhavaṃ. Ete saddā sakena sakena nāmena yathānuparodhena buddhasāsane pacchā puna nippajjante.

For these pronouns 'iya', 'ta', 'ma', 'ki', 'e', 'sa', the final vowel becomes long. Sometimes, for this root 'dusa', the vowel 'u' undergoes guṇa, the letter 'd' becomes 'r', and for the final 's' of the root, the substitutes 'sa', 'kkha', and 'ī' occur as is possible. These words, each with its own name, arise again later in the Buddha's teaching in due course.

Imamiva naṃ passatīti īdiso, yamiva naṃ passatīti yādiso, tamiva naṃ passatīti tādiso, mamiva naṃ passatīti mādiso, kimiva naṃ passatīti kīdiso, etamiva naṃ passatīti ediso, samānamiva naṃ passatīti sādiso[M 0.0298]. Imamiva naṃ passatīti īriso, yamiva naṃ passatīti yāriso, tamiva naṃ passatīti tāriso, mamiva naṃ passatīti māriso, kimiva naṃ passatīti kīriso, etamiva naṃ passatīti eriso, samānamiva naṃ passatīti sāriso. Imamiva naṃ passatīti īdikkho, yamiva naṃ passatīti yādikkho, tamiva naṃ passatīti tādikkho, evaṃ mādikkho, kīdikkho, edikkho, sādikkho. Īdī, yādī, tādī, mādī, kīdī, edī, sādī.

One sees him like this, thus 'īdiso'; one sees him like which, thus 'yādiso'; one sees him like that, thus 'tādiso'; one sees him like me, thus 'mādiso'; one sees him like what, thus 'kīdiso'; one sees him like this one, thus 'ediso'; one sees him as similar, thus 'sādiso'. One sees him like this, thus 'īriso'; one sees him like which, thus 'yāriso'; one sees him like that, thus 'tāriso'; one sees him like me, thus 'māriso'; one sees him like what, thus 'kīriso'; one sees him like this one, thus 'eriso'; one sees him as similar, thus 'sāriso'. One sees him like this, thus 'īdikkho'; one sees him like which, thus 'yādikkho'; one sees him like that, thus 'tādikkho'; similarly, 'mādikkho', 'kīdikkho', 'edikkho', 'sādikkho'. 'Īdī', 'yādī', 'tādī', 'mādī', 'kīdī', 'edī', 'sādī'.

Caggahaṇena tesameva saddānaṃ iyaiccevamādīnamanto ca saro kvaci dīghatthamāhu. Īdikkho, yādikkho, tādikkho, mādikkho, kīdikkho, edikkho, sādikkho. Idiso, sadiso, sariso, sarikkho.

By the inclusion of 'ca', it is said that the final vowel of those very words, such as 'iya', is also sometimes long. For example: 'īdikkho', 'yādikkho', 'tādikkho', 'mādikkho', 'kīdikkho', 'edikkho', 'sādikkho'. And 'idiso', 'sadiso', 'sariso', 'sarikkho'.

643, 635. Bhyādīhi mati budhi pūjādīhi ca tto.

From 'bhī' and other roots, and from roots with the sense of 'mati' (thinking), 'budhi' (knowing), 'pūjā' (honoring) and others, the suffix 'tta' occurs.

Bhīiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, mati. Budhi pūjādito ca tta paccayo hoti.

From roots such as 'bhī', and from roots with the meaning of 'mati' (thinking), 'budhi' (knowing), 'pūjā' (honoring), and so on, the suffix 'tta' occurs.

Bhāyitabboti bhīto, supitabboti sutto, mijjitabbo sinehetabboti mitto, sammannitabboti sammato, saṃ suṭṭhu mānitabbo pūjetabboti sammato, sammānīyitthāti sammato, saṃkappīyateti saṅkappito[M 0.0299], saṃkappīyitthāti saṅkappito, sampādīyateti sampādito, sampādīyitthāti sampādito, avadhārīyateti avadhārito, avadhārīyitthāti avadhārito, bujjhitabbo ñātabboti buddho, ajjhayitabboti ito, etabbo gantabboti ito, viditabbo ñātabboti vidito, takkīyateti takkito, pūjīyateti pūjito, pūjīyitthāti pūjito, apacāyitabboti apacāyito, mānitabbo pūjetabboti mānito, apacīyateti apacito, vandīyateti vandito, vandīyitthāti vandito, sakkarīyateti sakkārito, sakkarīyitthāti sakkārito.

That which is to be feared, thus 'bhīto' (frightened); that which is to be slept, thus 'sutto' (slept); that which is to be loved, thus 'mitto' (friend). That which is to be agreed upon, thus 'sammato' (agreed upon); that which is to be thoroughly honored and worshipped, thus 'sammato' (esteemed); it was thoroughly honored, thus 'sammato' (esteemed). It is thought upon, thus 'saṅkappito' (thought upon); it was thought upon, thus 'saṅkappito' (thought upon). It is brought about, thus 'sampādito' (brought about); it was brought about, thus 'sampādito' (brought about). It is ascertained, thus 'avadhārito' (ascertained); it was ascertained, thus 'avadhārito' (ascertained). That which is to be awakened and known, thus 'buddho' (awakened one); that which is to be studied, thus 'ito' (gone to for study); that which is to be gone, thus 'ito' (gone); that which is to be known, thus 'vidito' (known). It is reasoned about, thus 'takkito' (reasoned about); it is worshipped, thus 'pūjito' (worshipped); it was worshipped, thus 'pūjito' (worshipped). That which is to be revered, thus 'apacāyito' (revered); that which is to be honored and worshipped, thus 'mānito' (honored). It is revered, thus 'apacito' (revered); it is venerated, thus 'vandito' (venerated); it was venerated, thus 'vandito' (venerated). It is honored, thus 'sakkārito' (honored); it was honored, thus 'sakkārito' (honored).

644, 661. Vepu sī dava vamu ku dā bhū hvādīhi thu ttima ṇimā nibbatte.

From 'vepu', 'sī', 'dava', 'vamu', 'ku', 'dā', 'bhū', 'hu', and other roots, the suffixes 'thu', 'ttima', and 'ṇima' occur in the sense of 'derived from'.

Vepu sī dava vamu ku dā bhū huiccevamādīhi dhātūhi yathāsambhavaṃ thu ttima ṇimapaccayā honti nibbattatthe.

From roots such as 'vepu', 'sī', 'dava', 'vamu', 'ku', 'dā', 'bhū', 'hu', and others, the suffixes 'thu', 'ttima', and 'ṇima' occur as appropriate in the sense of derivation.

Vepanaṃ vepo, tena nibbatto vepathu, sayanaṃ sayo, tena nibbatto sayathu, davanaṃ davo, tena nibbatto davathu. Vamanaṃ vamo, tena nibbatto vamathu. Kutti karaṇaṃ, tena nibbattaṃ kuttimaṃ. Dāti dānaṃ, tena nibbattaṃ dattimaṃ. Bhūti bhavanaṃ, tena nibbattaṃ bhottimaṃ. Avahuti avahanaṃ, tena nibbattaṃ ohāvimaṃ.

'Vepana' (trembling) is 'vepo,' from which 'vepathu' (tremor) is derived. 'Sayana' (lying down) is 'sayo,' from which 'sayathu' (swelling) is derived. 'Davana' (burning) is 'davo,' from which 'davathu' (heat) is derived. 'Vamana' (vomiting) is 'vamo,' from which 'vamathu' (vomit) is derived. The act of making is 'kutti,' from which 'kuttimaṃ' (artificial) is derived. 'Dāti' (giving) is 'dāna,' from which 'dattimaṃ' (given) is derived. 'Bhūti' (being) is 'bhavana,' from which 'bhottimaṃ' (to be enjoyed) is derived. 'Avahuti' (offering) is 'avahana,' from which 'ohāvimaṃ' (what is offered) is derived.

645, 662. Akkose [M 0.0300] namhāni.

In the sense of abuse, 'na' and 'āni' are used.

Akkosaiccetasmiṃ atthe namhi paṭisedhayutte ānipaccayo hoti dhātūhi.

In this sense of 'abuse', when joined with the prohibitive particle 'na', the suffix 'āni' occurs after roots.

Na gamitabbaṃ agamāni te jamma desaṃ, na kattabbaṃ akarāṇi te jamma kammaṃ.

The meaning 'should not be gone' is expressed by 'agamāni', as in 'agamāni te jamma desaṃ' (May you not go to that wretched place, you wretch). The meaning 'should not be done' is expressed by 'akarāṇi', as in 'akarāṇi te jamma kammaṃ' (May you not do that wretched deed, you wretch).

Namhīti kimatthaṃ? Vipatti te jamma, vikati te jamma.

Why is 'with na' stated? For cases such as: 'Vipatti te jamma' (Misfortune to you, wretch), 'Vikati te jamma' (Perdition to you, wretch).

Akkoseti kimatthaṃ? Na gantabbā agati te.

Why is 'in the sense of abuse' stated? For cases such as: 'Na gantabbā agati te' (You should not go to a bad destination).

646, 419. Ekādito sakissa kkhattuṃ.

After 'eka' and other numerals, 'kkhattuṃ' is used in the sense of 'saki' (a time).

Ekādito sakissa kkhattuṃ hoti.

After 'eka' and other numerals, 'kkhattuṃ' occurs in the sense of 'saki'.

Ekassa padatthassa sakiṃ vāraṃ ekakkhattuṃ, dvinnaṃ padatthānaṃ sakiṃ vāraṃ dvikkhattuṃ, tiṇṇaṃ padatthānaṃ sakiṃ vāraṃ tikkhattuṃ, evaṃ catukkhattuṃ, pañcakkhattuṃ, chakkhattuṃ, sattakkhattuṃ, aṭṭhakkhattuṃ, navakkhattuṃ, dasakkhattuṃ. Iccevamādayo saddā yojetabbā.

For one item, one time is 'ekakkhattuṃ' (once); for two items, one time is 'dvikkhattuṃ' (twice); for three items, one time is 'tikkhattuṃ' (thrice); similarly, 'catukkhattuṃ' (four times), 'pañcakkhattuṃ' (five times), 'chakkhattuṃ' (six times), 'sattakkhattuṃ' (seven times), 'aṭṭhakkhattuṃ' (eight times), 'navakkhattuṃ' (nine times), 'dasakkhattuṃ' (ten times). Words such as these should be formed.

647, 663. Sunassunassoṇa vānuvānūnunakhunānā.

647, 663. For 'suna,' (the substitutes are) 'una,' 'oṇa,' 'vāna,' 'uvāna,' 'ūna,' 'unakha,' 'una,' 'ā,' 'ānā'.

Sunaiccetassa pāṭipadikassa unassa oṇa vāna uvāna ūna unakha una ā ānādesā honti.

For the stem 'suna,' the substitutions 'oṇa,' 'vāna,' 'uvāna,' 'ūna,' 'unakha,' 'una,' 'ā,' and 'ānā' occur.

Sāmikassa [M 0.0301] saddaṃ suṇātīti soṇo, sāmikassa saddaṃ suṇātīti svāno, evaṃ suvāno, sūno, sunakho, suno, sā, sāno.

One who hears the master’s sound is called 'soṇo'; one who hears the master’s sound is called 'svāno'; similarly, 'suvāno,' 'sūno,' 'sunakho,' 'suno,' 'sā,' and 'sāno'.

648, 664. Taruṇassa susu ca.

648, 664. For 'taruṇa,' also 'susu'.

Taruṇaiccetassa pāṭipadikassa susu ādeso hoti.

For the stem 'taruṇa,' the substitute 'susu' occurs.

Susu kāḷakeso.

'Susu' (a youth) has black hair.

649, 665. Yuvassuvassuvuvānunūnā.

649, 665. For 'yuva,' (the substitutes are) 'uva,' 'uva,' 'uvāna,' 'una,' 'ūnā'.

Yuvaiccetassa pāṭipadikassa uvassa uvauvāna unaūnādesā honti.

For the stem 'yuva,' the substitutions 'uva,' 'uva,' 'uvāna,' 'una,' and 'ūna' occur.

Yuvā, yuvāno, yuno, yūno.

Yuvā, yuvāno, yuno, yūno.

650, 651. Kāle vattamānātīte ṇvādayo.

650, 651. In the present and past tenses, (there are affixes) such as 'ṇu' and so on.

Kāle vattamānatthe ca atītatthe ca ṇu yu tapaccayā honti.

For expressing the present and past meanings, the suffixes 'ṇu,' 'yu,' and 'ta' occur.

Akāsi, karotīti kāru, agacchi, gacchatīti, vāyu, abhavi, bhavatīti bhūtaṃ.

'He made,' 'he makes'—thus 'kāru' (doer); 'he went,' 'he goes'—thus 'vāyu' (goer); 'he was,' 'he is'—thus 'bhūtaṃ' (being).

651, 647. Tavissati [M 0.0302] gamādīhi ṇī ghiṇa.

651, 647. In the future tense, from 'gam' and others, (the suffixes) 'ṇī,' 'ghi,' and 'ṇa' (occur).

Bhavissatikālatthe gamu bhaja su ṭhāiccevamādīhi dhātūhi ṇī ghiṇa paccayā honti.

For the future tense, the suffixes 'ṇī,' 'ghi,' and 'ṇa' occur from roots such as 'gam,' 'bhaj,' 'su,' 'ṭhā,' and others.

Āyatiṃ gamituṃ sīlaṃ yassa, so hotīti gāmī, āyatiṃ bhajituṃ sīlaṃ yassa, so hotīti bhājī, āyatiṃ passāpituṃ sīlaṃ yassa, so hotīti passāvi, āyatiṃ paṭṭhāyituṃ sīlaṃ yassa, so hotīti paṭṭhāyi.

One whose habit is to go in the future is 'gāmī'; one whose habit is to partake in the future is 'bhājī'; one whose habit is to cause to see in the future is 'passāvi'; one whose habit is to establish oneself in the future is 'paṭṭhāyi'.

652, 648. Kriyāyaṃ ṇvu tavo.

652, 648. In the sense of action, (the suffixes) 'ṇvu' and 'tav' (occur).

Kriyāyamatthe ṇvu tuiccete paccayā honti bhavissatikāle.

For the sense of action, the suffixes 'ṇvu' and 'tu' occur in the future tense.

“Karissa”nti kārako vajati, “bhuñjissa”nti bhottā vajati.

(Thinking,) 'I will do'—thus the doer proceeds; (thinking,) 'I will eat'—thus the enjoyer proceeds.

653, 306. Bhāvavācimhi catutthī.

653, 306. The dative case (occurs) in expressions of abstract nouns.

Bhāvavācimhi catutthīvibhatti hoti bhavissatikāle,

In the expression of abstract nouns, the dative case-ending occurs in the future tense.

Pacissate, pacanaṃ vā pāko, pākāya vajati. Bhuñjissate, bhojanaṃ vā bhogo, bhogāya vajati. Naccissate, naccanaṃ vā naccaṃ, naccāya vajati.

(In the sense of) 'he will cook,' the action is 'pacanaṃ' or 'pāko'; hence, 'he goes for cooking' ('pākāya vajati'). (In the sense of) 'he will eat,' the action is 'bhojanaṃ' or 'bhogo'; hence, 'he goes for enjoyment' ('bhogāya vajati'). (In the sense of) 'he will dance,' the action is 'naccanaṃ' or 'naccaṃ'; hence, 'he goes for dancing' ('naccāya vajati').

654, 649. Kammani [M 0.0303] ṇo.

654, 649. In the sense of the object, (the suffix) 'ṇa' (occurs).

Kammani upapade ṇapaccayo hoti bhavissatikāle.

When the object is the preceding word, the suffix 'ṇa' occurs in the future tense.

Nagaraṃ karissati nagarakāro vajati, sāliṃ lāvissati sālilāvo vajati, dhaññaṃ vapissati dhaññavāpo vajati, bhogaṃ dadissati bhogadāyo vajati, sindhuṃ pivissati sindhupāyo vajati.

(In the sense) 'he will build a city'—thus the city-builder proceeds; 'he will reap rice'—thus the rice-reaper proceeds; 'he will sow grain'—thus the grain-sower proceeds; 'he will give wealth'—thus the wealth-giver proceeds; 'he will drink the river'—thus the river-drinker proceeds.

655, 650. Sese ssaṃ ntumānānā.

655, 650. In the remaining senses, (the suffixes) 'ssaṃ,' 'ntu,' 'māna,' and 'āna' (occur).

Sesaiccetasmiṃ atthe ssaṃ ntu māna āna iccete paccayā honti bhavissatikāle kammūpapade.

For the remaining senses, the suffixes 'ssaṃ,' 'ntu,' 'māna,' and 'āna' occur in the future tense when the object is the preceding word.

Kammaṃ karissati kammaṃ karissaṃ, evaṃ kammaṃ karonto, kammaṃ kurumāno, kammaṃ karāno vajati. Bhojanaṃ bhuñjissati bhojanaṃ bhuñjissaṃ, evaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto, bhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno, bhojanaṃ bhuñjāno vajati. Khādanaṃ khādissati khādanaṃ khādissaṃ, evaṃ khādanaṃ khādanto, khādanaṃ khādamāno, khādanaṃ khādāno vajati. Maggaṃ carissati maggaṃ carissaṃ, evaṃ maggaṃ caranto, maggaṃ caramāno, maggaṃ carāno vajati. Bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissati bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissaṃ, evaṃ bhikkhaṃ bhikkhanto, bhikkhaṃ bhikkhamāno, bhikkhaṃ bhikkhāno vajati.

(In the sense) 'he will do the deed,' (the forms are) 'kammaṃ karissaṃ'; thus, 'kammaṃ karonto' (doing the deed), 'kammaṃ kurumāno' (performing the deed), 'kammaṃ karāno' (doing the deed), he proceeds. (In the sense) 'he will eat the meal,' (the forms are) 'bhojanaṃ bhuñjissaṃ'; thus, 'bhojanaṃ bhuñjanto' (eating the meal), 'bhojanaṃ bhuñjamāno' (consuming the meal), 'bhojanaṃ bhuñjāno' (eating the meal), he proceeds. (In the sense) 'he will chew the food,' (the forms are) 'khādanaṃ khādissaṃ'; thus, 'khādanaṃ khādanto' (chewing the food), 'khādanaṃ khādamāno' (munching the food), 'khādanaṃ khādāno' (chewing the food), he proceeds. (In the sense) 'he will walk the path,' (the forms are) 'maggaṃ carissaṃ'; thus, 'maggaṃ caranto' (walking the path), 'maggaṃ caramāno' (treading the path), 'maggaṃ carāno' (walking the path), he proceeds. (In the sense) 'he will beg for alms,' (the forms are) 'bhikkhaṃ bhikkhissaṃ'; thus, 'bhikkhaṃ bhikkhanto' (begging for alms), 'bhikkhaṃ bhikkhamāno' (seeking alms), 'bhikkhaṃ bhikkhāno' (begging for alms), he proceeds.

656, 666. Chavādīti [M 0.0304] tatraṇa.

656, 666. From 'cha' and others, (the suffixes) 'ta,' 'tra,' and 'ṇa' (occur).

Cha da ci ti su nī vi da pada tanu yata ada mada yuja vatumida mā pu ka la vara ve pu gupa dā iccevamādīhi dhātūhi tatraṇa iccete paccayā honti yathāsambhavaṃ.

From verbal roots such as 'cha,' 'da,' 'ci,' 'ti,' 'su,' 'nī,' 'vi,' 'da,' 'pad,' 'tan,' 'yat,' 'ad,' 'mad,' 'yuj,' 'vat,' 'mid,' 'mā,' 'pu,' 'ka,' 'la,' 'var,' 've,' 'pu,' 'gup,' 'dā,' and others, the suffixes 'ta,' 'tra,' and 'ṇa' occur as appropriate.

Ātapaṃ chādetīti chattaṃ, chatraṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ cintetīti cittaṃ, citraṃ. Cintenti sampayuttadhammā ethenāti vā cittaṃ, citraṃ. Atthe abhissavetīti suttaṃ, sutraṃ. Atthe sūcetīti vā suttaṃ, sutraṃ. Satte netīti nettaṃ, netraṃ. Satte icchitaṭṭhānaṃ nenti etenāti vā nettaṃ, netraṃ. Pakārena vidatīti pavittaṃ, pavitraṃ. Vividhena ākārena maṅga pāpaṃ punāti, sodhetīti pavittaṃ, pavitraṃ. Sucibhāvaṃ vā pāpuṇātīti pavittaṃ, pavitraṃ. Padati pāpuṇātīti patto, patro. Āhārā patanti ettha bhājaneti pattaṃ, patraṃ. Padati pavattatīti vā pattaṃ, patraṃ. Tanoti vitthāretīti tantaṃ, tantraṃ, tanitabbaṃ vitthāretabbanti vā tantaṃ, tantra. Yatatīti yattaṃ, yatraṃ. Yatati vīriyaṃ karoti etenāti vā yattaṃ, yatraṃ. Yatanaṃ vā yattaṃ, yatraṃ. Sukhadukkhaṃ adati bhakkhatīti attā, atrā. Madatīti mattaṃ, matraṃ. Vatthuṃ yujjanti etenāti yottaṃ, yotraṃ. Vattatīti vattaṃ, vatraṃ. Midati [M 0.0305] sinehaṃ karotīti mittaṃ. Mitraṃ. Midati sinehati etāyāti mettā, metrā. Pari samanta to sabbākārena minanti etāyāti mattā, matrā. Mānanaṃ vā mattaṃ, matraṃ. Attano kulaṃ punāti sodhetīti putto, putro. Kalitabbaṃ saṅkhyātabbanti kalattaṃ, kalatraṃ. Saṃsuṭṭhu vāreti etenāti varattaṃ, varatraṃ. Vepati kampatīti vettaṃ, vetraṃ. Gopitabbaṃ rakkhitabbanti guttaṃ. Gutraṃ, gottaṃ, gotraṃ. Dāti avakhaṇḍati etenāti dāttaṃ, dātraṃ iccevamādi.

It provides shade from the heat; thus, it is 'chattaṃ' or 'chatraṃ' (umbrella). It reflects upon its object; thus, it is 'cittaṃ' or 'citraṃ' (mind). Or, associated states contemplate through it; hence, it is 'cittaṃ' or 'citraṃ'. It proclaims the meaning; thus, it is 'suttaṃ' or 'sutraṃ' (thread). Or, it indicates meaning; thus, it is 'suttaṃ' or 'sutraṃ'. It leads beings; thus, it is 'nettaṃ' or 'netraṃ' (eye, guide). Or, they lead beings to the desired place through it; thus, it is 'nettaṃ' or 'netraṃ'. It purifies in a special way; thus, it is 'pavittaṃ' or 'pavitraṃ' (pure). It cleanses impurity and evil in manifold ways; thus, it is 'pavittaṃ' or 'pavitraṃ'. Or, it attains purity; thus, it is 'pavittaṃ' or 'pavitraṃ'. It goes or reaches; thus, it is 'patto' or 'patro'. Food falls into this vessel; thus, it is 'pattaṃ' or 'patraṃ' (bowl). Or, it moves forward; thus, it is 'pattaṃ' or 'patraṃ'. It extends and spreads; thus, it is 'tantaṃ' or 'tantraṃ' (thread, text); or, it is to be extended or spread out, thus it is 'tantaṃ' or 'tantra'. It strives; thus, it is 'yattaṃ' or 'yatraṃ' (effort). Or, one exerts energy through this; thus, it is 'yattaṃ' or 'yatraṃ'. Or, exertion itself is 'yattaṃ' or 'yatraṃ'. It consumes pleasure and pain; thus, it is 'attā' or 'atrā' (self). It is intoxicated; thus, it is 'mattaṃ' or 'matraṃ' (intoxicated). Things are joined by it; thus, it is 'yottaṃ' or 'yotraṃ' (yoke-tie). It revolves; thus, it is 'vattaṃ' or 'vatraṃ' (duty, cycle). It is affectionate; thus, it is 'mittaṃ' or 'mitraṃ' (friend). One is affectionate through this; thus, it is 'mettā' or 'metrā' (loving-kindness). They measure completely in every way through this; thus, it is 'mattā' or 'matrā' (measure). Or, measuring is 'mattaṃ' or 'matraṃ'. It purifies and cleanses one's family; thus, it is 'putto' or 'putro' (son). It is to be reckoned or counted; thus, it is 'kalattaṃ' or 'kalatraṃ' (wife). It restrains thoroughly through this; thus, it is 'varattaṃ' or 'varatraṃ' (strap). It trembles and shakes; thus, it is 'vettaṃ' or 'vetraṃ' (cane). It is to be guarded and protected; thus, it is 'guttaṃ' (protected), 'gutraṃ', 'gottaṃ', or 'gotraṃ' (lineage). It cuts and divides through this; thus, it is 'dāttaṃ' or 'dātraṃ' (sickle); and so on.

657, 667. Vadādīhi ṇitto gaṇe.

657, 667. From 'vad' and others, the suffix 'ṇitta' occurs in the sense of a group.

Vada cara varaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi ṇittapaccayo hoti gaṇatthe.

The suffix 'ṇitta' occurs from roots such as 'vad,' 'car,' 'var,' and others, in the sense of a group.

Vāditānaṃ gaṇo vādittaṃ. Evaṃ cārittaṃ, vārittaṃ, iccevamādi.

The group of musicians is 'vādittaṃ'. Similarly, 'cārittaṃ' (conduct), 'vārittaṃ' (restraint), and so forth.

658, 668. Midādīhi ttitiyo.

658, 668. From 'mid' and others, the suffixes 'tti' and 'ti' are applied.

Mida pada ranja tanu dhāiccevamādīhi dhātūhi tti ti iccete paccayā honti.

From the roots 'mid', 'pad', 'rañj', 'tan', 'dhā', and so on, these suffixes, namely 'tti' and 'ti', occur.

Midati sinehatīti metti, padati gacchatīti patti, ranjati etthāti ratti, tanoti vitthāretīti tanti, attano [M 0.0306] kulaṃ tanoti vitthāretīti vā tanti, paresaṃ itthīnaṃ puttaṃ dhāretīti dhāti, khīraṃ dhāretīti vā dhāti, attano sabhāvaṃ dhāretīti vā dhāti iccevamādi.

Because it is friendly or affectionate ('midati', 'sinehati'), it is 'metti' (friendship). Because it goes ('padati', 'gacchati'), it is 'patti' (attainment). Because one delights in it ('rañjati ettha'), it is 'ratti' (night). Because it stretches or spreads ('tanoti', 'vitthāreti'), it is 'tanti' (a thread). Or, 'tanti' is so called because it stretches or spreads one's own family ('attano kulaṃ tanoti', 'vitthāreti'). Because she bears a child for other women ('paresaṃ itthīnaṃ puttaṃ dhāreti'), she is a 'dhāti' (wet-nurse). Or, 'dhāti' is so called because she bears milk ('khīraṃ dhāreti'). Or, 'dhāti' is so called because she bears her own nature ('attano sabhāvaṃ dhāreti'). Thus and so forth.

659, 669. Usu ranja daṃsānaṃ daṃsassa daḍḍhoḍha ṭhā ca.

659, 669. For the roots 'us', 'rañj', and 'daṃs', 'daḍḍha' is the substitute for 'daṃs', and the suffixes 'ḍha' and 'ṭha' also occur.

Usu ranja daṃsaiccetesaṃ dhātūnaṃ daṃsassa daḍḍhādeso hoti, ḍha ṭhapaccayā ca honti.

For these roots, 'us', 'rañj', and 'daṃs', the substitution 'daḍḍha' occurs for 'daṃs', and the suffixes 'ḍha' and 'ṭha' also occur.

Usīyate uḍḍho, ranjanti etthāti raṭṭhaṃ, daṃsīyateti daḍḍho.

It is burned ('usīyate'), hence 'uḍḍho'. They delight in it ('rañjanti ettha'), hence 'raṭṭhaṃ' (a kingdom). It is bitten ('daṃsīyati'), hence 'daḍḍho'.

660, 670. Sūvusānamūvusānamatothoca.

660, 670. For 'sū', 'vu', and 'asa', 'ata' is the substitute for their 'ū', 'u', and 'asa', and 'tha' also occurs.

Sūvu asaiccetesaṃ dhātūnaṃ ūuasānaṃ atādeso hoti, thapaccayo ca.

For these roots, 'sū', 'vu', and 'asa', the substitution 'ata' occurs for 'ū', 'u', and 'asa', and the suffix 'tha' also occurs.

Savati hiṃsati etenāti satthaṃ, hirottappaṃ saṃvarati etenātivatthaṃ, saddānurūpaṃ asatibhavatīti attho,

That by which one harms ('savati', 'hiṃsati') is 'satthaṃ' (a weapon). That by which one restrains oneself with shame and fear of wrongdoing ('hirottappaṃ saṃvarati') is 'vatthaṃ' (a garment). 'Attho' (meaning) is so called because it becomes non-existent ('asati bhavati') in accordance with the word ('saddānurūpaṃ').

661, 671. Ranjudādīhi [M 0.0307] dha didda kirā kvaci jadalopoca.

661, 671. From 'rañj', 'ud', and so on, the affixes 'dha', 'da', 'idda', 'ka', and 'ira' are formed, and sometimes there is the elision of 'ja' and 'da'.

Ranja uda idi cadi madi khuda chidi rudi dala susa suca vaca vaja iccevamādīhi dhātūhi dha da idda ka iraiccete paccayā honti, kvaci ja da lopo ca, puna nippajjante.

From the roots 'rañj', 'ud', 'id', 'cad', 'mad', 'khud', 'chid', 'rud', 'dal', 'sus', 'suc', 'vac', 'vaj', and so on, these suffixes, namely 'dha', 'da', 'idda', 'ka', and 'ira', occur, and sometimes the elision of 'ja' and 'da' occurs, and they are formed anew.

Rañjitabbanti randhaṃ, ranjayitthāti vā randhaṃ, attani sannissitānaṃ macchamakarānaṃ pītisomanassaṃ undati pasavati janetīti samuddo, indati paramissariyaṃ karotīti indo, indattaṃ adhipatibhāvaṃ karotīti vā indo, canditabbo icchitabboti cando, mandati hāsetīti mando, maditabbo hāsetabboti vā mando, khudati pipāsetīti khuddo, chinditabboti chiddo, rudati hiṃsatīti ruddo, dalati duggatabhāvaṃ gacchatīti daliddo, sussatīti sukkaṃ, sucatītisoko, vacitabbanti vakkaṃ, appaṭihato hutvā vajati gacchatīti vajiraṃ iccevamādi.

That which is to be colored ('rañjitabbaṃ') is 'randhaṃ' (a fault). Or, that which one has colored ('rañjayittha') is 'randhaṃ'. The ocean ('samuddo') is so called because it moistens, brings forth, and generates ('undati', 'pasavati', 'janeti') joy and gladness for the fish and sea creatures dependent on it. 'Indo' (Indra) is so called because he exercises supreme power ('indati', 'paramissariyaṃ karoti'), or because he establishes lordship ('indattaṃ adhipatibhāvaṃ karoti'). The moon ('cando') is so called because it is to be desired ('canditabbo', 'icchitabbo'). 'Mando' (dull) is so called because it praises or gladdens ('mandati', 'hāseti'), or because it is to be praised or gladdened ('maditabbo', 'hāsetabbo'). 'Khuddo' (small) is so called because it is hungry or thirsty ('khudati', 'pipāseti'). 'Chiddo' (a hole) is so called because it is to be cut ('chinditabbaṃ'). 'Ruddo' (fierce) is so called because it harms ('rudati', 'hiṃsati'). 'Daliddo' (poor) is so called because one goes to a wretched state ('dalati', 'duggatabhāvaṃ gacchati'). 'Sukkaṃ' (dry) is so called because it dries up ('sussati'). 'Soko' (sorrow) is so called because one grieves ('sucati'). 'Vakkaṃ' (a kidney) is so called because it is to be spoken ('vacitabbaṃ'). 'Vajiraṃ' (a diamond) is so called because it goes without obstruction ('appaṭihato hutvā vajati', 'gacchati'). Thus and so forth.

662, 672. Paṭito hissa heraṇa hīraṇa.

662, 672. After 'paṭi', 'heraṇa' and 'hīraṇa' are substitutes for 'hissa'.

Paṭiiccetasmā hissa dhātussa heraṇa hīraṇa ādesā honti.

After 'paṭi', the substitutions 'heraṇa' and 'hīraṇa' occur for the root 'hissa'.

Paṭipakkhemadditvāgacchati pavattatīti pāṭiheraṃ, pāṭihīraṃ.

'Pāṭiheraṃ' or 'pāṭihīraṃ' (a miracle) is so called because, having crushed the opposition ('paṭipakkhe madditvā'), it comes forth and proceeds ('āgacchati', 'pavattati').

663, 673. Kaḍyādīhi [M 0.0308] ko.

663, 673. From 'kaḍi', etc., the suffix 'ka' occurs.

Kaḍi ghaḍi vaḍi karaḍi maḍi saḍi kuṭhi bhaḍi paḍi daḍi raḍi taḍi isiḍi caḍi gaḍi aḍi laḍi meḍi eraḍi khaḍi iccevamādīhi dhātūhi kapaccayo hoti saha paccayena ca nippajjante yathāsambhavaṃ.

From the roots 'kaḍi', 'ghaḍi', 'vaḍi', 'karaḍi', 'maḍi', 'saḍi', 'kuṭhi', 'bhaḍi', 'paḍi', 'daḍi', 'raḍi', 'taḍi', 'isiḍi', 'caḍi', 'gaḍi', 'aḍi', 'laḍi', 'meḍi', 'eraḍi', 'khaḍi', and so on, the suffix 'ka' occurs, and they are formed together with the suffix, as may be appropriate.

Kaṇḍitabbo chinditabboti kaṇḍo, ghaṇḍitabbo ghaṭetabboti ghaṇḍo, vaṇḍanti etthāti vaṇḍo, karaṇḍitabbo bhājetabboti karaṇḍo, maṇḍīyate vibhūsīyate etenāti maṇḍo, saṇḍanti gumbanti etthāti saṇḍo, aṅgamaṅgāni kuṇṭhati chindatīti kuṭṭhaṃ, bhaṇḍitabbanti bhaṇḍaṃ, paṇḍati liṅgavekallabhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṇḍako. Daṇḍati āṇaṃ karoti etenāti daṇḍo, raṇḍati hiṃsatīti raṇḍo, visesena taṇḍati cāleti paresaṃ viññūnaṃ hadayaṃ kampetīti vitaṇḍo, isiṇḍati paresaṃ maddatīti isiṇḍo, caṇḍati caṇḍikkabhāvaṃ karotīti caṇḍo, gaṇḍati sannicayati samūhaṃ karoti etthāti gaṇḍo, aṇḍīyati nibbattīyatīti aṇḍo, laṇḍitabbo jigucchitabboti laṇḍo, meṇḍati [M 0.0309] kuṭilabhāvaṃ gacchatīti meṇḍo, eraṇḍati rogaṃ hiṃsatīti eraṇḍo, khaṇḍitabbo chinditabboti khaṇḍo iccevamādi.

'Kaṇḍo' (an arrow) is so called because it is to be cut ('kaṇḍitabbo', 'chinditabbo'). 'Ghaṇḍo' (a bell) is so called because it is to be struck ('ghaṇḍitabbo', 'ghaṭetabbo'). 'Vaṇḍo' (a stalk) is so called because they thrive there ('vaṇḍanti ettha'). 'Karaṇḍo' (a basket) is so called because it is to be divided ('karaṇḍitabbo', 'bhājetabbo'). 'Maṇḍo' (scum, ornament) is so called because one is adorned or embellished by it ('maṇḍīyate', 'vibhūsīyate etena'). 'Saṇḍo' (a thicket) is so called because they cluster there ('saṇḍanti', 'gumbanti ettha'). 'Kuṭṭhaṃ' (leprosy) is so called because it cripples or cuts the limbs ('aṅgamaṅgāni kuṇṭhati', 'chindati'). 'Bhaṇḍaṃ' (goods) is so called because it is to be exchanged ('bhaṇḍitabbaṃ'). 'Paṇḍako' (a eunuch) is so called because one goes to a state of lacking gender characteristics ('paṇḍati', 'liṅgavekallabhāvaṃ gacchati'). 'Daṇḍo' (a staff) is so called because one exercises authority with it ('daṇḍati', 'āṇaṃ karoti etena'). 'Raṇḍo' (a cripple) is so called because it harms ('raṇḍati', 'hiṃsati'). 'Vitaṇḍo' (sophistry) is so called because it especially agitates, shakes, and makes tremble the hearts of other wise people ('visesena taṇḍati', 'cāleti paresaṃ viññūnaṃ hadayaṃ kampeti'). 'Isiṇḍo' is so called because it crushes others ('isiṇḍati', 'paresaṃ maddati'). 'Caṇḍo' (fierce) is so called because it creates a fierce state ('caṇḍati', 'caṇḍikkabhāvaṃ karoti'). 'Gaṇḍo' (a boil) is so called because it accumulates or forms a mass there ('gaṇḍati', 'sannicayati', 'samūhaṃ karoti ettha'). 'Aṇḍo' (an egg) is so called because it is produced ('aṇḍīyati', 'nibbattīyati'). 'Laṇḍo' (dung) is so called because it is to be loathed ('laṇḍitabbo', 'jigucchitabbo'). 'Meṇḍo' (a ram) is so called because it becomes crooked ('meṇḍati', 'kuṭilabhāvaṃ gacchati'). 'Eraṇḍo' (the castor-oil plant) is so called because it harms disease ('eraṇḍati', 'rogaṃ hiṃsati'). 'Khaṇḍo' (a piece) is so called because it is to be broken or cut ('khaṇḍitabbo', 'chinditabbo'). Thus and so forth.

664, 674. Khādāmagamānaṃ kha ndha’ndha gandhā.

664, 674. For 'khād', 'am', and 'gam', the substitutes are 'khandha', 'andha', and 'gandha'.

Khāda ama gamuiccetesaṃ dhātūnaṃ khandha andha gandhādesā honti, kapaccayo ca hoti.

For these roots, 'khād', 'am', and 'gam', the substitutions 'khandha', 'andha', and 'gandha' occur, and the suffix 'ka' also occurs.

Jātijarāmaraṇādīhi saṃsāradukkhehi khāditabboti khandho, amati aṅgamaṅgassa rujjanabhāvaṃ gacchatīti andho, cakkhunā amati rujjatīti vā andho, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ vātena gacchatīti gandho. Evaṃ khandhako, andhako, gandhako.

'Khandho' (an aggregate) is so called because it is to be devoured by the sufferings of saṃsāra, such as birth, aging, and death. 'Andho' (blind) is so called because one goes to a state of decay limb by limb ('amati aṅgamaṅgassa rujjanabhāvaṃ gacchati'), or because one goes to ruin by means of the eye ('cakkhunā amati rujjati'). 'Gandho' (smell) is so called because it goes to this or that place by means of the wind ('taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ vātena gacchati'). Similarly, 'khandhako', 'andhako', 'gandhako'.

665, 675. Paṭādīhyalaṃ.

665, 675. From 'paṭa', etc., the suffix 'ala' occurs.

Paṭa kala kusa kada bhaganda mekha vakka takka palla sadda mūla bila vida caḍaṃ pañca vā vasa paci maca musa gotthu puthu bahu maṅga baha kamba samba aggaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi pāṭi padikehi ca uttarapadesu alapaccayo hoti, pacchā puna nippajjante.

From the roots and nominal stems 'paṭa', 'kala', 'kusa', 'kada', 'bhaganda', 'mekha', 'vakka', 'takka', 'palla', 'sadda', 'mūla', 'bila', 'vida', 'caḍaṃ', 'pañca', 'vā', 'vasa', 'paci', 'maca', 'musa', 'gotthu', 'puthu', 'bahu', 'maṅga', 'baha', 'kamba', 'samba', 'agga', and so on, the suffix 'ala' occurs in the second part of a compound, and they are subsequently formed anew.

Paṭe alanti paṭalaṃ, kale alanti kalalaṃ, pāpake akusale dhamme kusati chindatīti kusalaṃ, kusabhūte yathāsabhāvadhamme alanti vā kusalaṃ, kuse uddissa dāne alanti vā kusalaṃ, kuse sañcaye dhammasamudāye alanti [M 0.0310] vā kusalaṃ, kadde madde alanti kadalaṃ, bhagande secane alanti bhagandalaṃ, bhagande muttakarīsaharaṇe alanti vā bhagandalaṃ, mekhe kaṭivicitte alanti mekhalaṃ, vakke rukkhatace alanti vakkalaṃ, takke rukkhasilese alanti takkalaṃ, palle ninnaṭṭhāne alanti pallalaṃ, sadde harite alanti saddalaṃ, mūle patiṭṭhāne alanti mulālaṃ, biḷe nissaye alanti bilālaṃ, vide vijjamāne alanti vidalaṃ, caṇḍe alanti caṇḍālo, pañcannaṃ rājūnaṃ alanti pañcālo, vā gatigandhanesu alanti vālaṃ, vā padagamane alanti vā vāḷo, vase acchādane alanti vasalo, pace vitthāre alanti pacalo, mace corakamme alanti macalo, muse theyye, muse pāṇacāge vā alanti musalo, gotte vaṃse siṅgālajātiyaṃ alanti gotthulo, puthumhi vitthāre alanti puthulo, bahumhi saṅkhyāne alanti bahulo, bahumhi vuddhimhi alanti vā bahulo, maṅgamhi gamane alanti maṅgalaṃ, bahumhi vuddhimhi alanti bahalaṃ, kambamhi sañcalane alanti [M 0.0311] kambalaṃ. Sambamhi maṇḍale alanti sambalaṃ, agge gatikoṭille alanti aggaḷaṃ. Iccevamādayo aññepi saddā bhavanti.

'Paṭalaṃ' (a covering) is so called because it is fit for a cloth ('paṭe alanti'). 'Kalalaṃ' (an embryo) is so called because it is fit for its time ('kale alanti'). 'Kusalaṃ' (wholesome) is so called because it cuts off evil, unwholesome things ('pāpake akusale dhamme kusati chindati'). Or, 'kusalaṃ' is so called because it is fit for things that have become as they are by nature ('kusabhūte yathāsabhāvadhamme alanti'). Or, 'kusalaṃ' is so called because it is fit for giving with kusa grass in mind ('kuse uddissa dāne alanti'). Or, 'kusalaṃ' is so called because it is fit for the collection of dhammas in a heap of kusa grass ('kuse sañcaye dhammasamudāye alanti'). 'Kadalaṃ' (a plantain) is so called because it is fit for mud ('kadde madde alanti'). 'Bhagandalaṃ' (a fistula) is so called because it is fit for discharge ('bhagande secane alanti'), or because it is fit for the removal of urine and feces ('bhagande muttakarīsaharaṇe alanti'). 'Mekhalaṃ' (a girdle) is so called because it is fit for a waist-ornament ('mekhe kaṭivicitte alanti'). 'Vakkalaṃ' (bark) is so called because it is fit for the bark of a tree ('vakke rukkhatace alanti'). 'Takkalaṃ' (bark) is so called because it is fit for the resin of a tree ('takke rukkhasilese alanti'). 'Pallalaṃ' (a small pond) is so called because it is fit for a low place ('palle ninnaṭṭhāne alanti'). 'Saddalaṃ' (a grassy spot) is so called because it is fit for greenness ('sadde harite alanti'). 'Muḷālaṃ' (a lotus root) is so called because it is fit for a root or foundation ('mūle patiṭṭhāne alanti'). 'Biḷālo' (a cat) is so called because it is fit for a hole or support ('biḷe nissaye alanti'). 'Vidalaṃ' (a splinter) is so called because it is fit for what exists ('vide vijjamāne alanti'). 'Caṇḍālo' (an outcaste) is so called because he is fit for fierceness ('caṇḍe alanti'). 'Pañcālo' (the Pañcāla people) is so called because it is fit for five kings ('pañcannaṃ rājūnaṃ alanti'). 'Vālaṃ' (hair) is so called because it is fit for movement and smells ('vā gatigandhanesu alanti'), or 'vāḷo' (a beast) is so called because it is fit for going on foot ('vā padagamane alanti'). 'Vasalo' (an outcaste) is so called because he is fit for covering ('vase acchādane alanti'). 'Pacalo' (trembling) is so called because it is fit for expansion ('pace vitthāre alanti'). 'Macalo' (a thief) is so called because he is fit for thievery ('mace corakamme alanti'). 'Musalo' (a pestle) is so called because it is fit for theft ('muse theyye alanti'), or because it is fit for taking life ('muse pāṇacāge alanti'). 'Gotthulo' (a jackal) is so called because it is fit for a lineage, family, or the jackal species ('gotte vaṃse siṅgālajātiyaṃ alanti'). 'Puthulo' (broad) is so called because it is fit for breadth ('puthumhi vitthāre alanti'). 'Bahulo' (abundant) is so called because it is fit for a large number ('bahumhi saṅkhyāne alanti'), or because it is fit for growth ('bahumhi vuddhimhi alanti'). 'Maṅgalaṃ' (auspicious) is so called because it is fit for going ('maṅgamhi gamane alanti'). 'Bahalaṃ' (thick) is so called because it is fit for growth ('bahumhi vuddhimhi alanti'). 'Kambalaṃ' (a blanket) is so called because it is fit for shaking ('kambamhi sañcalane alanti'). 'Sambalaṃ' (provisions) is so called because it is fit for a circle ('sambamhi maṇḍale alanti'). 'Aggaḷaṃ' (a bolt) is so called because it is fit for crooked movement ('agge gatikoṭille alanti'). Thus, there are these and other such words.

666, 676. Puthassa puthu pathā mo vā.

666, 676. For 'putha', the substitutions are 'puthu' and 'patha', or the suffix 'ma' occurs.

Puthaiccetassa pāṭipadikassa puthu pathādesā honti, kvaci amapaccayo hoti.

For this nominal stem 'putha', the substitutions 'puthu' and 'patha' occur, and sometimes the suffix 'ama' occurs.

Putha hutvā jātanti puthavī pathame jāto pathamo, pathavī, paṭhamo vā, puthu kilese janetīti puthujjano, puthu hutvā jātanti pathavī, pathavī vā.

'Puthavī' (the earth) is so called because it is born having become broad ('putha hutvā jātaṃ'). 'Pathamo' (the first) is so called because he is born first ('pathame jāto'). Or, 'pathavī', or 'paṭhamo'. 'Puthujjano' (an ordinary person) is so called because he generates various ('puthu') defilements ('kilese janeti'). 'Pathavī' (the earth) is so called because it is born having become broad ('puthu hutvā jātaṃ'), or 'pathavī'.

667, 677. Sasvādīhi tu davo.

667, 677. From sasu, etc., the suffixes tu and du occur.

Sasu dada ada madaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi tu duiccete paccayā honti.

From the roots sasu, dada, ada, mada, and so on, these suffixes, namely tu and du, occur.

Aññe satte sasati hiṃsatīti sattu, dukkhaṃ dadātīti daddu, dukkhena adati bhakkhati etthāti addu, dukkhaṃ adati anubhavati jano etenāti vā addu, dukkhaṃ bhājanaṃ [M 0.0312] ādhāraṃ bhāvatīti vā addu, madati ummattaṃ karotīti maddu, madati maddabhāvaṃ karotīti vā maddu.

Sattu (enemy) is so called because he harms other beings (aññe satte sasati, hiṃsati). Daddu (ringworm) is so called because it gives suffering (dukkhaṃ dadāti). Addu (a kind of disease or pain) is so called because one eats or consumes in suffering herein (dukkhena adati, bhakkhati ettha), or because people experience suffering through it (dukkhaṃ adati, anubhavati jano etena), or because it becomes a vessel and basis of suffering (dukkhaṃ bhājanaṃ ādhāraṃ bhavati). Maddu (intoxication or pride) is so called because it intoxicates (madati, ummattaṃ karoti), or because it causes a state of intoxication (madati, maddabhāvaṃ karoti).

668, 678. Jhādīhi īvaro.

668, 678. From jhā, etc., the suffix īvara occurs.

Ci pā dhāiccevamādīhi dhātūhi īvarapaccayohoti.

From the roots ci, pā, dhā, and so on, the suffix īvara occurs.

Cīyatīti cīvaraṃ, pivatīti pīvaro, pātabbaṃ rakkhitabbanti vā pīvaraṃ. Dhāreti dhāretvā jīvitaṃ kappetīti dhīvaro, dhīvaraṃ.

Cīvara (robe) is so called because it is accumulated (cīyati). Pīvara (fat, stout) is so called because one drinks (pivati), or because it is to be drunk and preserved (pātabbaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ). Dhīvara (fisherman) is so called because he supports his life (dhāreti, dhāretvā jīvitaṃ kappeti).

669, 679. Munādīhi ci.

669, 679. From muna, etc., the suffix i occurs.

Muna yata agga pata kava suca ruca mahāla bhaddāla manaiiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, pāṭipadikehi ca ipaccayo hoti.

From the roots muna, yata, agga, pata, kava, suca, ruca, mahāla, bhaddāla, mana, and so on, and also from nominal stems, the suffix i occurs.

Atthānatthaṃ munāti, ñeyyadhammaṃ lakkhaṇādivasena vā jānātīti muni, yatati vīriyaṃ karotīti yati, aggati kuṭilabhāvaṃ gacchatīti aggi, patati seṭṭho hutvā purato gacchatīti pati, kabyaṃ bandhatīti kavi, kantaṃ manāpavacanaṃ vadatīti vā kavi. Sucati parisuddhaṃ bhavatīti suci, rucati dibbatīti ruci, mahantaṃ vibhāvaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ lātīti mahāli, bhaddaṃ yasaṃ lātīti bhaddāli, manaṃ tattha ratane nayatīti maṇi.

One who understands what is beneficial and harmful, or knows knowable things by way of characteristics, is called a muni. One who strives, makes effort, is called a yati. One who goes to crookedness is called aggi. One who, being the best, goes forward is called pati. One who composes poetry is called kavi. Or one who speaks pleasing and agreeable words is called kavi. One who becomes pure is called suci. One who shines brightly is called ruci. One who obtains great and extensive possessions is called mahāli. One who obtains auspicious fame is called bhaddāli. That which leads the mind to that jewel is called maṇi.

670, 680. Vidādīhyūro[M 0.0313].

670, 680. From vida, etc., the suffix ūra occurs.

Vida valla masa sida dukukapu maya udi khajja kuraiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, pāṭipadikehi ca ūrapaccayohoti.

From roots such as vida, valla, masa, sida, du, ku, kapu, maya, udi, khajja, kura, and so on, and also from nominal stems, the suffix ūra occurs.

Vidituṃ alanti vidūro, vidūraṭṭhāne jāto vedūro, vallati vallabhāvena bhavatīti vallūro, vallati aññamaññaṃ bandhatīti vā vallūro, āmasitabboti masūro, sindati siṅgārabhāvaṃ gacchatīti sindūro, sindati virocatīti vā sindūro, gamituṃ alaṃ anāsannattāti dūro, kuti saddaṃ karotīti kūro, attano gandhena aññaṃ gandhaṃ kapati hanati hiṃsatīti kappūro, kappati rogāpanayane samatthetīti vā kappūro, mahiyaṃ ravatīti mayūro, mahiyaṃ yāti gacchatīti mayūro, paṃsuṃ undati pasavatīti undūro, khajjitabbo khāditabboti khajjūro, kurati akkosatīti kurūro.

One who is able to know is called vidūro. One who is born in a distant place is called vedūro. That which pleases by being dear is called vallūro. Or that which binds mutually is called vallūro. That which is to be touched is called masūro. That which goes to a state of adornment or love is called sindūro. Or that which shines brightly is called sindūro. That which is able to be gone to because of not being near is called dūro. That which makes a sound is called kūro. That which covers, destroys, or injures another scent with its own scent is called kappūro. Or that which is capable of removing disease is called kappūro. That which cries on the earth is called mayūro. That which goes on the earth is called mayūro. That which throws up dust is called undūro. That which is to be eaten is called khajjūro. That which scolds is called kurūro.

671, 681. Hanādīhi nu ṇutavo.

671, 681. From hana, etc., the suffixes nu, ṇu, and tu occur.

Hana jana bhāri khanu ama ve vedhā siki hi iccevamādīhi dhātūhi nu ṇu kuiccete paccayā honti.

From roots such as hana, jana, bhāri, khanu, ama, ve, vedha, siki, hi, and so on, the suffixes nu, ṇu, and ku occur.

Bhojanaṃ [M 0.0314] hanati hiṃsati etenāti haṇu, hanu vā. Gamanaṃ janetītī jāṇu, bhāṇu dibbatīti bhāṇu, nivāte riti gacchatītī reṇu, khaṇitabbo avadāritabboti khāṇu. Aṅgamaṅgassa rujjanabhāvaṃ vijjhanabhāvaṃ amati gacchatīti aṇu, veṇu, veti tantasantāne bhavatītī veṇu, bahisārealantivāveṇu vacchaṃ, pāyetītī dhenu, atthaṃ dhāretītī dhātu, gamanapacanādikaṃ kriyaṃ dhāretītī vā dhātu, sīyatī bandhīyatītī setu, uddhaṃ gacchati pavattatītī ketu, attano phalaṃ hinoti pavattatītī hetu.

That by which food is destroyed or injured is called haṇu or hanu. That which produces movement is called jāṇu. That which shines is called bhāṇu. That which moves in the absence of wind is called reṇu. That which is to be dug up or split open is called khāṇu. That which goes, causing a state of pain or piercing to every limb, is called aṇu. That which exists in a continuity of threads is called veṇu. Or that which is able outside the enclosure is also called veṇu. That which causes to drink is called dhenu. That which holds meaning is called dhātu. Or that which holds actions like going and cooking is also called dhātu. That which is bound or tied is called setu. That which goes or proceeds upward is called ketu. That which impels or produces its own fruit is called hetu.

672, 682. Kuṭādīhi ṭho.

672, 682. From kuṭa, etc., the suffix ṭha occurs.

Kuṭa kusa kaṭaiccevamādīhi dhātūhi, pāṭipadikehi ca ṭhapaccayo hotī.

From roots such as kuṭa, kusa, kaṭa, and so on, and also from nominal stems, the suffix ṭha occurs.

Aṅgamaṅgaṃ kuṭati chindatītī kuṭṭhaṃ, dhaññena chādetabbo pūretabbotī koṭṭho, kaṭitabbaṃ madditabbanti, kaṭṭhaṃ.

That which cuts or severs limb by limb is called kuṭṭhaṃ (leprosy). That which is to be covered and filled with grain is called koṭṭho (granary). That which is to be crushed and pounded is called kaṭṭhaṃ (wood).

673, 683. Manu pūra suṇādīhi ussa nusisā.

673, 683. From manu, pūra, suṇa, etc., the suffixes usa, nusa, and isa occur.

Manu pūra suṇa kusu ila ala maha si ki iccevamādīhi dhātūhi, pāṭipadikehi ca usa nusa isaiccete paccayā honti, puna nippajjante.

From roots such as manu, pūra, suṇa, kusu, ila, ala, maha, si, ki, and so on, and also from nominal stems, these suffixes, namely usa, nusa, and isa, occur, and they are formed again.

Kusalākusale [M 0.0315] dhamme manati jānātīti manusso, mānuso. Kāraṇā kāraṇaṃ manati jānātīti vā manusso, mānusso. Atthānatthaṃ manati jānātīti vā manusso, mānusso. Mātāpitūnaṃ hadayaṃ pūretīti puriso, attano manorathaṃ pūretīti vā puriso, pūretīti vā poso, sasurehi suṇitabbā hiṃsitabbāti suṇisā, dvinnaṃ jānānaṃ kulasantānaṃ karotīti vā suṇisā, kucchitabbanti karīsaṃ, gabbhaṃ vimocetīti suriso, tamandhakāravidhamanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ surati hiṃsatīti sūriyo, rogaṃ hiṃsatīti sirīso, ilati kampatīti illiso, taṇhāya dubbalo hutvā ilati kampatīti vā illigho, pāpakaraṇe alati samatthetīti alaso, mahitabbo pūjetabboti mahiso, sīyati bandhīyatīti sīsaṃ, kitabbaṃ hiṃsitabbanti kisaṃ, iccevamādi.

One who knows wholesome and unwholesome states is called a manusso or mānuso. Or one who knows cause and non-cause is called a manusso or mānuso. Or one who knows what is beneficial and not beneficial is called a manusso or mānuso. One who fulfills the hearts of his parents is called a puriso. Or one who fulfills his own desires is called a puriso. Or one who fills or nourishes is called a poso. She who is to be heard from and harmed by her in-laws is called a suṇisā. Or she who creates the family lineage of two peoples is called a suṇisā. That which is to be despised is called karīsaṃ. One who releases from the womb is called a suriso. That which, by dispelling darkness, destroys the fear of beings is called the sūriyo. That which destroys disease is called sirīso. One who trembles and shakes is called illiso. Or one who, weakened by craving, trembles and shakes is called illigho. One who is capable of doing evil is called alaso. One who is to be honored and revered is called a mahiso. That which is bound is called the sīsaṃ. That which is to be treated and is harmed is called kisaṃ. And so on.

Iti kibbidhānakappe uṇādikappo chaṭṭho kaṇḍo.

Thus, in the chapter on verbal derivatives, the chapter on Uṇādi is the sixth section.

Uṇādikappo niṭṭhito.

The chapter on Uṇādi is completed.

Kaccāyanapakaraṇaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Kaccāyana Treatise is completed.
